title: AI Summarization Prompts That Keep the Key Points Intact
excerpt: Learn how to write AI summarization prompts that control length, audience and focus, with copy-ready templates for articles, reports and long documents.
seo_title: AI Summarization Prompts for Long Text and Reports
seo_description: Write better AI summarization prompts: set length, audience and focus, avoid lost details, and use copy-ready templates for articles, reports and notes.

faq.q: How do I make an AI summary shorter without losing key points?
faq.a: Give a hard limit such as five bullets or 100 words, and tell the AI what must survive: decisions, numbers, definitions or conclusions. A limit alone forces vague writing. A limit plus priorities forces useful compression.

faq.q: Can AI summarize a document I paste in?
faq.a: Yes, if the text fits the tool's input limit. For very long documents, split the text into sections, summarize each, then ask for a summary of the summaries. Always check the result against the original for important details.

faq.q: Why does my AI summary sound generic?
faq.a: Generic summaries usually come from generic prompts. If you do not state the audience, purpose and focus, the AI defaults to a vague overview. Tell it who the summary is for and what decision or task it should support.

faq.q: Is it okay to rely on an AI summary for studying?
faq.a: Use it as a map, not a replacement. A summary helps you decide what to read closely, but exams and assignments test understanding. Read the source for anything important and check claims the summary makes.

content:
A good summarization prompt tells the AI three things: who the summary is for, how long it should be, and which details must not be dropped. Without those, you get a vague paragraph that sounds fine and helps nobody.

Summarizing is one of the most common uses of AI tools, and one of the easiest to do badly. The model will happily compress anything, but compression always means choosing what to leave out. Your prompt decides what gets cut.

## Why most summaries disappoint

When you paste a long text and type "summarize this," the model has to guess your purpose. Is this for a quick skim, a briefing for your manager, or revision notes? Each needs different content. The usual failures are:

- **Too generic.** The summary restates the topic but loses the argument.
- **Wrong emphasis.** Minor examples survive while the main conclusion disappears.
- **Missing specifics.** Dates, numbers, names and conditions get smoothed into "various factors."
- **Added content.** Occasionally the model adds a claim that was never in the source.

Every one of these is a prompt problem you can reduce.

## The four controls of a summary prompt

### 1. Audience

State who will read the result. A summary for a busy executive differs from one for a ninth-grade student. Try "for a reader with no background in the topic" or "for a manager who has two minutes."

### 2. Length and shape

Be exact. "Five bullet points," "three sentences," or "a 150-word paragraph" all work better than "short." You can also ask for a layered shape: a one-sentence takeaway first, then supporting bullets.

### 3. Focus

Tell the AI what to prioritize: the main argument, the methods, the decisions made, the action items, or the risks. If you only need one angle, say so.

### 4. Fidelity rules

Add a line such as "Use only information from the text. If something is unclear, say so instead of guessing." This reduces invented detail.

## A reusable summary template

Copy this and fill in the brackets.

```
You are helping me understand a text quickly.

Audience: [who will read this]
Purpose: [what they will do with it]
Length: [exact format, e.g. 5 bullets + one-sentence takeaway]
Priorities: [what must be kept: conclusions, numbers, deadlines, definitions]

Rules:
- Use only information in the text below.
- Keep all numbers, dates and names exactly as written.
- If the text is unclear or incomplete on a point, say "unclear in source."

Text:
[paste text]
```

## Summaries for different situations

### Articles and reports

Ask for the thesis, the three strongest supporting points, and any limits the author admits. That gives you the argument rather than a topic list.

### Meeting notes and transcripts

Ask for decisions, owners and deadlines in a table, followed by open questions. Summaries of conversations fail when they narrate the discussion instead of capturing outcomes.

### Textbook chapters

Ask for key terms with one-line definitions, then a short explanation of how the ideas connect. Follow up with "quiz me on this" to turn passive reading into practice.

### Legal, medical or financial documents

An AI summary can help you navigate the structure, but it is not professional advice. Use it to prepare questions, and confirm anything consequential with a qualified person.

## Handling very long documents

Models have input limits, and quality can drop when a prompt is huge. A dependable method is chunking:

1. Split the document into logical sections, such as chapters or headings.
2. Summarize each section with the same template so the outputs are consistent.
3. Paste the section summaries into a new prompt and ask for a combined summary.
4. Ask which sections contained details that were hardest to compress, then re-read those yourself.

This two-pass approach keeps each step small enough to check.

## Checking the summary

A summary you have not verified is a draft. Use these quick checks:

- Pick three specific claims from the summary and find them in the source.
- Ask the AI: "List any statement in your summary that is not directly supported by the text."
- Compare numbers and names against the original.
- Ask "What important point from the text is missing from this summary?" and see whether the answer matters.

## A second-pass prompt that improves quality

After the first summary, try:

```
Rewrite the summary so a reader could act on it without opening the original.
Add anything essential that is missing, but stay within [word limit].
Mark any claim you are less than certain about with [check].
```

The "[check]" marker gives you a short list of places to verify instead of rereading everything.

## A worked example

Imagine you have a 3,000-word article about remote work policies and you need to brief a team lead before a meeting. A weak prompt says "summarize this article." A stronger one reads: "Summarize for a team lead who has not read the article and must decide whether to change our remote policy. Give a one-sentence takeaway, then four bullets covering the main findings, the strongest argument for change, the strongest argument against, and any limits the author admits. Keep every number exactly as written."

The second prompt produces something the team lead can use in the meeting, because it is built around the decision rather than the topic. Notice how each instruction removes a guess the model would otherwise make for you.

## Different summary shapes for different jobs

Not every summary should be a paragraph. Pick the shape that serves the reader:

- **Executive brief:** takeaway, three supporting points, recommended action.
- **Study notes:** key terms, main ideas and one example per idea.
- **Comparison summary:** a table placing two sources side by side on the same questions.
- **Timeline summary:** events in order with dates, useful for history and project updates.
- **Question-driven summary:** answer three specific questions you wrote, ignoring everything else.

The last shape is underused. If you know what you need from a text, list the questions and ask the model to answer them from the text only. This avoids the usual problem of a summary that covers everything and answers nothing.

## Common mistakes

- **Asking for "a summary" with no limit.** The model picks a length that suits itself.
- **Skipping the audience.** The tone and vocabulary will not fit your reader.
- **Trusting numbers blindly.** Models can slip on figures when compressing; verify them.
- **Summarizing instead of reading in high-stakes cases.** For contracts, research you will cite, or safety information, read the source.
- **Pasting copyrighted or confidential material carelessly.** Check the rules of your tool and your workplace first.
- **Submitting a summary as your own analysis.** Summaries support learning; they do not replace your own work, and many schools and employers expect disclosure of AI use.

## Next steps

title: AI Prompts for Rewriting and Editing Your Own Writing
excerpt: Use AI as an editor, not a ghostwriter. Learn rewriting and proofreading prompts that fix clarity, tone and flow while keeping your voice and meaning intact.
seo_title: AI Prompts for Rewriting and Editing Your Writing
seo_description: Use AI prompts to rewrite and edit your own writing: improve clarity, tone and flow, keep your voice, and avoid over-polished robotic text. Templates inside.

faq.q: How do I get AI to edit without changing my voice?
faq.a: Tell it explicitly: fix errors and unclear sentences only, keep my word choices and sentence rhythm where possible. Paste a short sample of your normal writing as a style reference and ask it to match that sample.

faq.q: What is the best prompt to proofread text?
faq.a: Ask for a list of corrections rather than a rewritten version: show each original phrase, the fix and a short reason. That keeps you in control and lets you accept or reject each change.

faq.q: Why does AI-edited writing sound robotic?
faq.a: Open-ended prompts like 'make this better' push the model toward polished but generic phrasing. Give a target tone, a reader and a list of things to avoid, and edit in small sections instead of whole documents.

faq.q: Should I tell people I used AI to edit my work?
faq.a: Follow the rules of your school, employer or publication. Light grammar help is often acceptable, but some places require disclosure. When in doubt, ask, and never present AI-written text as your own where that is prohibited.

content:
To get useful editing from AI, ask for specific changes to text you already wrote, and say what must stay the same. "Make this better" invites a full rewrite in the model's default voice. "Fix grammar and cut repetition, but keep my wording" gets you an editor.

This guide covers prompts for proofreading, tightening, tone changes and structural feedback, plus ways to keep your own voice.

## Decide what kind of edit you need

Editing is not one task. Naming the level of edit is the single biggest improvement you can make.

- **Proofreading:** spelling, grammar, punctuation, typos.
- **Copyediting:** consistency, clarity, awkward phrasing, repetition.
- **Line editing:** sentence rhythm, word choice, tone.
- **Developmental editing:** structure, argument, what is missing or in the wrong order.

If you ask for all four at once, the model blends them and you cannot tell what changed. Run them one at a time, starting from the top (structure) down to proofreading last.

## Proofreading without rewriting

For a safe pass, request a change list instead of a new draft.

```
Proofread the text below. Do NOT rewrite it.
Return a table with three columns: Original, Suggested fix, Reason.
Only include real errors in spelling, grammar, punctuation or word misuse.
Do not change style or word choice. If something is only a matter of taste, ignore it.

Text:
[paste]
```

Because you see each change, you can accept some and reject others. This also teaches you your own recurring mistakes.

## Tightening and clarity

Wordy writing is common and easy to fix with constraints.

```
Edit the paragraph for clarity and concision.
- Cut filler words and repeated ideas.
- Keep every fact and my main meaning.
- Keep my vocabulary where it is already clear.
- Aim for roughly 20% fewer words.
Show the edited version, then list what you removed in one line.
```

That last line, "list what you removed," is a useful guardrail. If the model deleted something that mattered, you will spot it.

## Changing tone on purpose

Tone shifts are a natural fit for AI. Be concrete about the destination and the reader.

```
Rewrite this email for a senior manager I have not met.
Tone: respectful, direct, warm but not casual.
Keep it under 120 words. Keep the request in the first two sentences.
Do not add facts that are not in my draft.
```

Useful pairs to try: formal to friendly, technical to plain-language, long to scannable, blunt to diplomatic. Ask for two options in different tones and combine the parts you like.

## Keeping your own voice

Voice is mostly rhythm, word choice and what you leave unsaid. Models smooth all of that out unless you protect it.

1. **Give a sample.** Paste two or three paragraphs you wrote and ask the model to describe your style in a few bullet points.
2. **Reuse that description.** Add "Edit in this style" with the bullet points to later prompts.
3. **Work in small pieces.** A paragraph at a time keeps changes visible.
4. **Add a ban list.** Tell it to avoid phrases you dislike, such as stock openers or buzzwords.

## Getting structural feedback

Before polishing sentences, check whether the piece works.

```
Act as an editor reading my draft for the first time.
Reader: [who]. Goal of the piece: [what it should achieve].
Tell me:
1. The main point as you understand it, in one sentence.
2. Where you lost interest or got confused.
3. Anything missing the reader would expect.
4. Paragraphs I could cut or reorder.
Do not rewrite anything yet.
```

If the model's one-sentence summary does not match what you meant, the draft has a clarity problem that sentence-level editing will not fix.

## A simple editing workflow

1. Write your draft yourself, even if it is rough.
2. Ask for structural feedback and make changes by hand.
3. Run a tightening pass and review each change.
4. Run a proofreading pass with the change-list prompt.
5. Read the final text aloud. If any sentence feels foreign, rewrite it in your words.

Reading aloud catches the places where polished phrasing no longer sounds like you.

## Editing for non-native writers

AI can be a helpful language coach. Ask it to explain why a correction was made, for example: "For each fix, give a one-line grammar note so I can learn the rule." Over time you need fewer corrections, which is more valuable than a clean draft you could not have written yourself.

## Rewriting for a new purpose

Sometimes you are not fixing a draft but repurposing it: turning a report into an email, a long email into a short message, or an essay paragraph into a presentation slide. The risk is that meaning drifts. Protect it with a short "must keep" list.

```
Turn the text below into [NEW FORMAT] for [READER].
Must keep: [3 to 5 facts or points that cannot change].
May cut: examples, background and anything repetitive.
Do not add claims. After the rewrite, list anything from the original you left out.
```

The closing request lets you see what was dropped, which is usually where a repurposed piece goes wrong.

## A before and after illustration

Consider a sentence such as: "We are writing to inform you that, due to the fact that the project has been delayed, the delivery date will be moved to a later point in time." A light edit prompt might return: "The project has been delayed, so delivery will move to a later date." Better still, if you supply the real date, the final line becomes specific: "Delivery is now 14 March."

The lesson is that AI can remove clutter quickly, but only you can supply the missing fact that makes the sentence useful. When the edit exposes a gap like this, fill it yourself rather than letting the model invent a plausible detail.

## Common mistakes

- **Pasting a whole document and saying "improve."** You will get a different document.
- **Not saying what must stay.** Facts, names, quotes and numbers can be altered during rewriting. State that they must remain unchanged and check them.
- **Accepting every suggestion.** Treat output as proposals. You are the author.
- **Letting the model add claims.** Rewrites sometimes insert plausible but unsupported statements. Add "do not add new information."
- **Ignoring policies.** Schools, publishers and employers may restrict AI-assisted writing. Use AI to improve your own work and follow the rules that apply to you.
- **Over-polishing.** Perfectly smooth text with no personality reads as generic. Keep some of your natural edges.

## Next steps

title: Brainstorming Prompts That Produce Better Ideas With AI
excerpt: Move past bland idea lists. Use constraint-based brainstorming prompts, idea filters and follow-up questions to get fresher, more usable ideas from any AI tool.
seo_title: Brainstorming Prompts That Get Better Ideas From AI
seo_description: Get better ideas from AI with brainstorming prompts that use constraints, personas, idea filters and follow-ups. Includes copy-ready templates for any project.

faq.q: Why does AI give boring brainstorming ideas?
faq.a: A vague request returns the most common answers, because those are the most likely patterns. Add constraints, a specific audience and a request for unusual angles, then ask for ideas you would not normally consider.

faq.q: How many ideas should I ask for?
faq.a: Ask for 10 to 15 in the first round so you see variety, then pick two or three and ask for development. Asking for 50 at once usually produces repetition and filler in the later half.

faq.q: Can AI replace human brainstorming?
faq.a: It is a good partner for volume and variation, but it does not know your situation unless you tell it. Use it to widen your options, then apply your own judgment, experience and taste to choose.

faq.q: How do I avoid copying existing ideas?
faq.a: Treat AI output as raw material. Combine ideas, change the audience or context, and research whether something similar exists before you publish or build. Original work comes from your selection and development.

content:
To get better brainstorming results from AI, give it constraints, context and a way to judge ideas, instead of asking for "ideas about X." Constraints push the model off the obvious answers, and a filtering step turns a long list into a short, usable one.

Brainstorming is where AI feels easiest and where lazy prompts give the most forgettable output. Here is a repeatable method.

## Why unconstrained brainstorming fails

Language models predict likely text. Ask for "blog ideas about fitness" and you receive the ideas that appear most often in everyone's writing: "10 tips for beginners," "benefits of morning workouts." They are not wrong, just interchangeable.

Constraints move the model into less crowded territory. So does context about you: your audience, limits, skills and goals.

## The four-part brainstorming prompt

1. **Goal:** what the ideas are for and what success looks like.
2. **Context:** who it is for, what you already have, what you tried.
3. **Constraints:** budget, time, tools, tone, things to avoid.
4. **Output format:** how many, how detailed, how organized.

```
I need ideas for [project].
Goal: [what success looks like]
Audience: [who]
What I already have: [skills, tools, existing content]
Constraints: [time, budget, things to avoid]

Give me 12 ideas. Make at least 4 of them unconventional.
For each: a one-line description and why it fits my constraints.
Do not repeat the obvious ideas everyone suggests.
```

## Techniques that widen the range

### Force different angles

Ask the model to approach the same problem from separate viewpoints.

- "Give 3 ideas each from the perspective of a beginner, an expert and a skeptic."
- "Give ideas that cost nothing, ideas that need a small budget, and ideas that need a team."
- "Give one idea per month of the year."

### Use inversion

Ask what would guarantee failure, then flip it. "List 10 ways to make my newsletter boring, then turn each into an idea for making it engaging." This often surfaces overlooked problems.

### Combine unrelated things

Pick two unrelated fields and ask for overlaps: "Combine [study skills] with [game design] and propose five classroom activities." Forced mashups are a classic creativity method and work well with AI.

### Change the constraint

Take your best idea and tighten a limit: "Now do it in one afternoon," or "Now do it with no screen." Constraints often produce stronger ideas than freedom.

## Turn a long list into a short one

Generating is easy. Choosing is the real work. Ask the model to help you evaluate, then make the decision yourself.

```
Here are my ideas: [paste].
Score each from 1 to 5 on:
- Fit with my goal
- Effort required
- Originality
- Risk
Show a table, then recommend the top 3 and explain the trade-offs.
Flag any idea that might closely resemble something already common.
```

Scores from a model are opinions, not measurements. Use them to structure your thinking, then adjust with what you know.

## Develop the winners

Once you pick two or three ideas, go deeper.

- "Turn idea 4 into a one-page plan with first steps for this week."
- "List the three biggest assumptions behind this idea and how I could test each cheaply."
- "Play a critic: give the strongest objections to this idea."
- "Suggest a version for a different audience."

This moves you from a list to a plan.

## Brainstorming for students and teachers

Brainstorming prompts are useful for project topics, research questions and activity design. A student can ask for ten possible angles on a broad topic, then choose one and research it personally. A teacher can ask for five ways to teach one concept using different materials. The key responsible habit: use AI to explore options, then do the thinking, research and writing yourself.

## Iterate in conversation

A single prompt rarely gives the best ideas. Treat the exchange as a back-and-forth:

1. Get a first batch.
2. React honestly: "I like 3 and 7 because they are practical. 5 is too expensive. Give 8 more like 3 and 7."
3. Ask for a hybrid of two favorites.
4. Ask what is missing from the whole list.

Telling the model what you liked is more effective than restating the whole request.

## Keep a record

Save prompts that produced good ideas. When you build a [personal prompt library](/blog), brainstorming templates are among the most reusable, because you only change the project and constraints.

## Worked example: a school project

Say a student must choose a science fair project and has a limited budget, two weeks and a shared kitchen as a lab. A bare prompt like "science fair ideas" returns the volcano and the plant-growth test. A constrained prompt does better: "I need science fair project ideas for ages 13 to 14. Budget under a small amount, two weeks, household materials only, safe without adult chemistry supervision. Give 10 ideas, at least 4 that measure something unusual, and for each name the one variable I would change and the one I would measure."

The final clause forces each idea to be testable, which is what a science fair judge actually cares about. Notice that the prompt shaped the ideas, but the student still chooses, tests and writes up the project personally.

## Group brainstorming with AI

In a team, AI can act as an extra participant rather than a replacement for discussion. Have everyone write ideas privately first, so the group is not anchored by the first suggestion. Then paste the combined list and ask the model to cluster similar ideas, point out gaps and suggest two directions nobody mentioned. Finally, discuss as humans and vote. This keeps the diversity of your team while using AI for the tedious sorting.

## A quick brainstorming checklist

Before you send the prompt, confirm that you have named the goal, the audience and at least two real constraints. After the first batch, look for repetition: if five ideas are variations of one, ask for options from a completely different category. Before you commit to an idea, test it with one cheap experiment, such as showing a sketch to a friend or drafting a single page, so that you learn from reality rather than from the model's enthusiasm.

## Common mistakes

- **Asking for ideas with no context.** The model cannot know your skills, audience or limits.
- **Accepting the first list.** The first batch is usually the most predictable.
- **Asking for too many ideas.** Quality drops and repetition rises.
- **Skipping evaluation.** A list is not a decision.
- **Treating AI ideas as automatically original.** Check whether something similar already exists, especially for names, slogans and products.
- **Outsourcing the thinking.** The value comes from your selection and development, not from the raw list.

## Next steps

Explore creative and planning prompts in the [productivity prompt collection](/prompts/category/productivity), design a custom brainstorming prompt in the [prompt builder](/prompt-builder), or browse the full [prompt library](/prompts).

title: How to Extract Data Into Tables With AI Prompts Safely
excerpt: Turn messy text, emails and notes into clean tables with AI. Learn prompts that define columns, handle missing values and let you verify every extracted row.
seo_title: Extract Data Into Tables With AI Prompts: A Guide
seo_description: Learn how to extract data into tables with AI prompts: define columns, handle missing values, request CSV or Markdown output, and verify every row.

faq.q: What is the best format to ask AI for table output?
faq.a: Markdown tables are easy to read in chat, and CSV is best for pasting into a spreadsheet. State the format explicitly, list the exact column names, and ask for no extra commentary around the table.

faq.q: How do I stop AI from inventing missing values?
faq.a: Tell it to write 'not stated' for any field the text does not contain, and never to infer or estimate. Adding a source-quote column makes unsupported entries easy to spot.

faq.q: Can AI extract data from many documents at once?
faq.a: It can, but accuracy falls as batches grow. Process a few items at a time using the same column definitions, then combine the tables and spot-check a sample against the originals.

faq.q: Is AI extraction accurate enough to trust?
faq.a: It is good for a first pass but not error-free, especially with numbers and ambiguous wording. Spot-check rows, validate totals, and verify anything used for decisions, grading, finance or compliance.

content:
To extract data into a table with AI, define the exact columns, say what to do when information is missing, and request a specific output format. Then verify a sample of rows against the source. Done this way, a few minutes of prompting can replace an hour of copy and paste.

This works for emails, job postings, product descriptions, survey comments, reading lists, schedules and meeting notes.

## What AI extraction is good at

Models are strong at reading messy human text and fitting it into a consistent structure. Typical jobs:

- Pull names, dates, amounts and deadlines from emails.
- Turn a job description into a table of skills, requirements and benefits.
- Convert a list of references into columns for author, year, title and source.
- Sort survey comments into themes with counts.
- Compare several products against the same attributes.

It is weaker at exact arithmetic, long tables with hundreds of rows, and text where meaning is truly ambiguous. Keep that in mind when deciding how much to trust the output.

## The anatomy of an extraction prompt

A reliable prompt has five parts:

1. **Task:** "Extract the following fields from the text."
2. **Schema:** exact column names, each with a short definition and allowed values.
3. **Rules for gaps:** what to write when data is absent or unclear.
4. **Output format:** Markdown table, CSV or JSON.
5. **Source text:** clearly separated from the instructions.

```
Extract information from the text below into a Markdown table.

Columns:
- Name: person or organization
- Date: in YYYY-MM-DD format
- Amount: number only, no currency symbol
- Currency: 3-letter code if stated
- Action needed: one short phrase
- Source quote: the exact words that support this row

Rules:
- Use only what is in the text. Never guess.
- If a field is missing, write "not stated".
- One row per item. Do not merge items.
- Return only the table.

Text:
<<<
[paste]
>>>
```

The delimiter lines around the text help the model separate your instructions from the content, which matters when the text itself contains instructions or questions.

## Define each column tightly

Vague column names produce inconsistent answers. Compare "Date" with "Deadline date, YYYY-MM-DD, not the email sent date." Where possible, give allowed values: "Priority: High, Medium or Low only." Allowed lists make sorting and filtering afterward trivial.

## Choose the right output format

- **Markdown table:** best for reading in chat or pasting into documents.
- **CSV:** best for spreadsheets. Ask for a header row and say that fields containing commas must be quoted.
- **JSON:** best if the output goes into code. Specify the keys and types.

If a table will be pasted into a spreadsheet, test a small batch first. A stray comma or line break can shift columns.

## Build verification into the prompt

The "Source quote" column in the example above is the most useful trick in this article. It forces the model to point at evidence, and lets you check each row in seconds. If the quote does not say what the row says, the row is wrong.

Further checks you can add:

- "Add a Confidence column: High, Medium or Low."
- "Add a Notes column for anything ambiguous."
- "After the table, list any rows where you had to interpret wording."

Confidence labels are not statistically meaningful, but they help you decide where to look first.

## Working with larger batches

Accuracy drops when prompts get long. A better routine:

1. Test the prompt on three to five items and refine the columns.
2. Process the rest in small batches with the identical prompt.
3. Merge the tables in a spreadsheet.
4. Check totals, duplicates and blank cells with spreadsheet formulas, not the AI.
5. Spot-check a random sample against the originals.

Do arithmetic in the spreadsheet. Models can miscount and mis-add, so let software handle sums and averages.

## Turning comments into themes

Qualitative data, such as open-ended survey answers, can be coded into categories.

```
Below are 20 survey comments. Create a table with:
Comment number | Theme | Sentiment (positive, neutral, negative) | Short reason.
Use no more than 6 themes and reuse the same theme names consistently.
Then list the themes with the number of comments for each.
```

Review the themes yourself. The labels are the model's interpretation, and a different reader might group comments differently.

## Privacy and data handling

Before pasting emails, student records, customer lists or any personal data into an AI tool, remove names, contact details and identifiers, or use a tool your organization has approved. Replace real names with codes such as "Person A." See our guide on [privacy-safe prompting](/blog) for a fuller checklist.

## Worked example: job postings to a comparison table

Suppose you saved five job postings and want to compare them. Paste each posting and use a fixed schema: Role title, Company, Location or remote, Required skills (list), Nice-to-have skills, Experience level, Salary if stated, Application deadline, and Source quote for the requirements. Add the rule "write not stated for anything missing."

With the same schema applied to every posting, you can sort by required skills, spot recurring requirements and see which gaps in your résumé matter most. You can then run your résumé through the [ATS resume checker](/ats-resume-checker) against the postings you care about. The table is only as honest as the extraction, so check the source quotes for the roles you are most interested in.

## Cleaning and normalizing values

Raw data is inconsistent: "Jan 5", "5/1/24" and "5th January" all mean the same thing, or maybe not, depending on the date format. Add normalization rules to your prompt, such as "convert all dates to YYYY-MM-DD; if the day and month are ambiguous, write ambiguous and keep the original text." Do the same for names, currencies and units. Where you cannot define a rule, ask the model to list the ambiguous values and resolve them yourself.

## A quick extraction checklist

Before you trust a table, run through these checks. Does every row have a source quote? Are there any cells that look suspiciously complete, given that the text was thin? Do dates and numbers use one consistent format? Are duplicates merged or flagged? Did you compare at least a few rows with the original text? If any answer is no, fix it before the data goes into a report, a grade book or a decision.

## Common mistakes

- **Not defining columns.** The model invents its own, differently each time.
- **Leaving gaps unaddressed.** Without a rule, models often fill blanks with plausible guesses.
- **Trusting numbers.** Verify totals and figures, especially in finance or grading contexts.
- **Mixing instructions and text.** Use clear delimiters.
- **Using huge batches.** Smaller batches are easier to verify and usually more accurate.
- **Skipping spot checks.** A table that looks neat can still contain errors.

title: AI Prompts for Building Lesson Plans and Course Outlines
excerpt: Build clear lesson plans and course outlines with AI. Use prompts that set objectives, timing, activities and assessment, then adapt the draft to your class.
seo_title: AI Prompts for Lesson Plans and Course Outlines
seo_description: Use AI prompts to draft lesson plans and course outlines with objectives, timing, activities and assessments. Templates for teachers, tutors and trainers.

faq.q: Can AI write a complete lesson plan?
faq.a: It can draft a solid structure with objectives, activities and timing, but it does not know your students, curriculum standards or classroom resources. Treat the output as a first draft and adapt it to your context.

faq.q: What details should I include in a lesson plan prompt?
faq.a: Include grade or level, subject, topic, lesson length, learning objectives, class size, available materials, prior knowledge, and any learner needs. The more specific the context, the more usable the plan.

faq.q: How do I make AI lesson plans align with standards?
faq.a: Paste the specific standard or objective text from your official curriculum into the prompt and ask the plan to address it. Then check the alignment yourself, since models can misread or misquote standards.

faq.q: Can I use AI to create assessments for my lesson?
faq.a: Yes. Ask for questions tied to each objective, with an answer key and marking guidance. Review them for accuracy, difficulty and fairness before use, because AI-generated questions can contain mistakes.

content:
To build a useful lesson plan with AI, give it your level, topic, time, objectives and constraints, then ask for a timed structure with activities and a check for understanding. The result is a draft you refine, not a finished plan.

The same method works for course outlines, workshop agendas and training sessions, so teachers, tutors and corporate trainers can all use it.

## What to tell the AI first

Lesson plans fail when the prompt is only "make a lesson plan on photosynthesis." The model fills in everything else with generic assumptions. Provide:

- **Level and subject:** grade, age range or course level.
- **Topic and scope:** what is in and what is out.
- **Time:** total length, for example 45 minutes.
- **Objectives:** what learners should be able to do by the end.
- **Prior knowledge:** what they already know.
- **Class context:** size, available materials, technology access, learner needs.
- **Format preferences:** group work, discussion, hands-on, minimal prep.

## A copy-ready lesson plan prompt

```
Create a lesson plan.

Subject and level: [e.g. Grade 7 science]
Topic: [specific topic]
Length: [minutes]
Learning objectives (use action verbs): [list or ask me to propose 3]
Prior knowledge: [what students already know]
Materials available: [list]
Class: [size, any support needs]

Structure the plan with timings:
1. Opening hook (with a question or short task)
2. Direct instruction (key ideas in plain language)
3. Guided practice
4. Independent or group activity
5. Check for understanding (3 questions)
6. Closing and homework suggestion

Also include: likely misconceptions and how to address them,
one extension task for fast finishers, one support strategy for learners who struggle.
Keep the teacher prep under 20 minutes.
```

## Write objectives that can be measured

Objectives guide everything else. Weak: "Understand fractions." Stronger: "Compare two fractions with different denominators and explain which is larger." Ask the AI to rewrite vague goals using action verbs such as explain, compare, solve, classify or justify. Then ask it to match each activity to an objective. Any activity that serves no objective can be cut.

## Course outlines and unit sequences

For a longer course, work top-down.

1. **Define the outcome:** what a learner can do at the end of the course.
2. **Ask for modules:** "Propose 6 modules in a logical order, with a one-line goal each."
3. **Check the sequence:** "Which modules depend on earlier ones? Point out any ordering problems."
4. **Expand one module at a time** into lessons, activities and assessments.
5. **Add pacing:** map modules to weeks and flag where review time is needed.

Going module by module keeps quality higher than requesting a full 12-week syllabus in one prompt.

## Assessment and feedback

Ask for assessments tied to the objectives you set.

```
Write 5 questions that check objective 2 of this lesson.
Mix 3 multiple-choice and 2 short-answer.
Provide an answer key and a simple marking guide.
Make wrong options reflect common misconceptions.
```

Always read every question and answer. AI-generated quiz items sometimes have two correct answers, an incorrect key or unclear wording.

## Adapting for different learners

A strong second prompt is adaptation: "Adjust the activity for learners with limited English," "Provide a version with simpler reading," or "Suggest a low-tech alternative with no devices." You can also ask for different ways to explain the same idea, such as an analogy, a worked example or a diagram description.

## Aligning with standards

If you must meet a curriculum standard, paste its exact wording and ask the plan to address it. Then verify alignment yourself. Models may paraphrase or invent standard codes, so do not rely on codes the AI supplies without checking your official documents.

## Review checklist before using the plan

- Is every fact correct for your level?
- Are the timings realistic for your actual class?
- Does each activity connect to an objective?
- Are materials available and safe?
- Does it include a real check for understanding, not just a final quiz?
- Does it fit your school's policies and curriculum?

## Keeping teaching human

AI can save planning time, but the strongest lessons come from what you know about your students: their interests, their struggles and their questions. Use the draft as scaffolding. Add local examples, change what will not work and keep the parts that sound like you.

## Worked example: a 45-minute science lesson

A teacher of 12-year-olds wants to teach the idea that heat moves from hot objects to cooler ones. The prompt specifies the level, the 45-minute slot, three action-verb objectives (describe, predict, explain), prior knowledge of temperature, and materials: cups, warm water and thermometers. The AI returns a timeline: a five-minute hook asking why a metal spoon feels colder than a wooden one, ten minutes of instruction, a fifteen-minute paired experiment, and a ten-minute exit check.

The draft is a useful skeleton. The teacher then adjusts what the AI cannot know: that the thermometers are scarce, that two students need reading support, and that the fire safety rules forbid hot water above a certain temperature. Those local edits are the professional judgment that turns a generic plan into a good lesson.

## Differentiation and pacing tips

Ask for pacing flags directly: "Mark which activities can be shortened if we run late and which cannot be skipped." You can also request tiered tasks, with the same core question at three levels of challenge, so all students work on the same idea. For tutors working one-to-one, change the prompt to ask for diagnostic questions first, so the session starts from what the learner actually knows.

## Adapting for tutors, trainers and parents

The same prompts work outside school classrooms. A tutor can ask for a single-session plan built around a learner's recent mistakes. A workplace trainer can request a ninety-minute workshop with a short exercise after each concept and a feedback form. A parent teaching at home can ask for a week of short activities that fit around meals and chores, using household materials. In each case, state the learner's actual starting point and the time available, and ask for the simplest plan that could work, since a short plan that is followed beats an ambitious one that is abandoned.

## Common mistakes

- **Skipping learner context.** Generic plans do not fit real classes.
- **Packing too much in.** Models tend to overfill lessons; remove content to leave time for practice.
- **Accepting incorrect content.** Verify every fact, formula and example.
- **No assessment.** Without a check for understanding, you cannot tell whether the lesson worked.
- **Using unvetted questions.** Test items need review before students see them.
- **Sharing student data.** Do not paste names or private information into AI tools.

## Next steps

Explore ready-made classroom resources in the [education prompts](/prompts/category/education), shape your own request with the [prompt builder](/prompt-builder), or browse additional [AI tools](/ai-tools) for teachers.

title: How to Reduce AI Hallucinations With Better Prompts
excerpt: AI can state false things with confidence. Learn prompt techniques that reduce hallucinations: grounding, permission to say 'I don't know', and source checks.
seo_title: Reduce AI Hallucinations With Better Prompts
seo_description: Learn practical prompt techniques to reduce AI hallucinations: ground answers in your text, allow 'I don't know', ask for evidence, and verify what matters.

faq.q: What is an AI hallucination?
faq.a: A hallucination is output that sounds confident and fluent but is false, unsupported or invented, such as a made-up source, statistic or quote. It happens because models generate likely text rather than looking up verified facts.

faq.q: Can prompts completely stop hallucinations?
faq.a: No. Good prompts reduce the risk, but no prompt removes it. Grounding the answer in text you supply helps most, and you should still verify facts, names, numbers and citations that matter.

faq.q: Why does AI make up sources and citations?
faq.a: Only a little. A vague plea for accuracy changes less than structural instructions do, such as supplying the source text, allowing uncertainty, limiting the scope and requesting evidence for each claim you can check yourself.

faq.q: Does asking AI to be accurate help?
faq.a: Only a little. A vague plea for accuracy changes less than structural instructions: supply the source text, allow uncertainty, limit the scope and request evidence for each claim you can then check yourself.

content:
You can reduce AI hallucinations by giving the model source material to work from, allowing it to say "I don't know," limiting the scope of its answer and asking for evidence you can check. You cannot eliminate them, so verification remains your job.

A hallucination is a confident statement that is false or unsupported. It might be an invented statistic, a fake citation, a wrong date or a plausible but untrue explanation. Understanding why it happens makes the fixes make sense.

## Why models hallucinate

A language model generates text by predicting what is likely to come next. It does not look facts up in a verified database unless a tool is connected for that. When it lacks information, it can still produce fluent text that fits the pattern of a correct answer. Risk rises when:

- the question is about obscure or very recent topics,
- you ask for specific numbers, quotes, dates or citations,
- your prompt assumes something false,
- the answer needs long, multi-step reasoning,
- the model feels pressure to answer rather than admit uncertainty.

## Technique 1: Ground the answer in supplied text

The strongest method is to paste the relevant material and instruct the model to rely only on it.

```
Answer the question using ONLY the text between <<< and >>>.
If the text does not contain the answer, reply exactly: "Not found in the provided text."
Do not use outside knowledge.

Text:
<<<
[paste source]
>>>

Question: [your question]
```

This turns an open-ended recall task into a reading task, which models handle far better. Remember that it only helps if your source is correct.

## Technique 2: Give permission to be uncertain

Models often behave as though an answer is required. Make "I don't know" an acceptable response.

- "If you are not sure, say so and explain what is uncertain."
- "Separate what you are confident about from what you are guessing."
- "Do not guess names, numbers, dates or sources."

Even so, the model's stated confidence is not a reliable measure. Treat "I am confident" as a style, not a guarantee.

## Technique 3: Narrow the scope

Broad questions invite filling gaps. Compare "Tell me about the causes of this historical event" with "List three commonly cited causes, one sentence each, and note where historians disagree." The second limits the model to claims it can state carefully and invites nuance.

Break complex questions into smaller ones, check each answer, then combine them.

## Technique 4: Ask for evidence you can inspect

When using supplied text, ask for quotes.

```
For each claim in your answer, include the exact supporting quote from the text.
If you cannot quote support, remove the claim.
```

For general-knowledge questions, ask the model to separate claims into "well established," "debated" and "unsure," then check the shaky ones with trusted sources. If you want sources, ask for the kinds of sources to search for, such as "textbooks, official statistics agencies, peer-reviewed reviews," rather than specific citations the model may invent.

## Technique 5: Remove false assumptions

Leading questions can trigger hallucination. "Why did the 2010 study prove X?" assumes a study exists. Rephrase neutrally: "Is there research on X? What is known, and what is uncertain?" Also ask the model to check your premise: "Before answering, tell me if my question contains any assumption that might be wrong."

## Technique 6: Use a second pass as a checker

After an answer, run a review prompt.

```
Review your previous answer.
1. List every factual claim as a numbered list.
2. Mark each as: verifiable from the provided text / general knowledge / uncertain.
3. Point out any claim that might be invented or outdated.
```

This does not guarantee correctness, because the same model can repeat the same error, but it often exposes weak claims worth checking. Pair it with your own verification, covered in our guide to [fact-checking AI outputs](/blog).

## Matching the technique to the task

| Situation | Best approach |
|---|---|
| Summarizing a document | Ground in text, require quotes |
| General explanation | Narrow scope, flag uncertainty |
| Needing sources | Ask for source types, find them yourself |
| Numbers and dates | Verify against an official source |
| Creative writing | Hallucination is less of a concern; facts still need checks |

## High-risk areas

Be extra careful with health, legal, financial and safety topics, academic citations, and anything that will be published or graded. In those cases, use AI to understand and prepare questions, then rely on qualified professionals and primary sources.

## Settings and tools

Some tools offer web search or document upload that can ground answers in real sources, and some have settings that affect randomness. Features and names change, so check the official help pages of the tool you use. Even with search enabled, open the cited pages to confirm they say what the answer claims.

## A habit that helps

Make a short routine: supply source text when you can, require "not found" for gaps, ask for quotes, and verify the three most important claims independently. It takes a couple of minutes and prevents most embarrassing errors.

## A before and after example

Weak prompt: "What did the 2019 study on sleep and exam performance conclude, and who wrote it?" This presumes a specific study and asks for names, which invites an invented answer.

Stronger prompt: "I am looking for research on sleep and exam performance. Do not name specific studies or authors from memory. Tell me what the general findings are, what is still debated, and what search terms and databases I could use to find primary research."

The second version gives up on the fragile details and keeps the useful part. You then find real studies yourself, read them and, if you wish, paste the text back in for a grounded summary. This pattern, from memory to search to supplied text, is the most dependable route to accurate work.

## Signs an answer deserves extra scrutiny

Certain features raise the odds of a hallucination. Be wary when the answer includes unusually precise figures with no origin, a perfect quote, a named expert you have not heard of, a source with no link or identifiable publisher, or a confident explanation of something very recent or very niche. Another sign is an answer that agrees with whatever you suggested. If you ask "isn't it true that X?" and the model enthusiastically confirms, rephrase the question neutrally and see whether the answer changes. An answer that flips with your wording was not anchored to facts.

## Common mistakes

- **Trusting fluent answers.** Smooth writing is not evidence of truth.
- **Using made-up citations.** Always locate sources yourself.
- **Asking for precise figures from memory.** Numbers are a frequent failure point.
- **Writing leading questions.** Premises sneak falsehoods in.
- **Believing "be accurate" fixes everything.** Structure beats pleading.
- **Skipping verification on important work.** The higher the stakes, the more checking you need.

## Next steps

See research-friendly templates in the [student prompts](/prompts/category/students), build a grounded prompt using the [prompt builder](/prompt-builder), or explore trusted [AI tools](/ai-tools) that support document upload.

title: How to Fact-Check AI-Generated Answers Step by Step
excerpt: Never publish or submit AI output unchecked. Follow a practical fact-checking workflow: pick claims, trace sources, cross-check, and record what you verified.
seo_title: How to Fact-Check AI-Generated Answers Step by Step
seo_description: A practical workflow to fact-check AI answers: isolate claims, find primary sources, cross-check numbers and quotes, and log what you verified before using it.

faq.q: Can I ask AI to fact-check its own answer?
faq.a: It can help list claims and flag shaky ones, but it can repeat its own mistakes with confidence. Use it to organize the checking, then confirm claims against independent, reliable sources yourself.

faq.q: What should I always verify in AI output?
faq.a: Verify names, dates, numbers, quotes, citations, legal or medical statements, and any claim your work depends on. Also check anything surprising, since a striking fact is often where an error hides.

faq.q: How many sources do I need to confirm a fact?
faq.a: For routine facts, one reliable primary or authoritative source may do. For contested or important claims, check at least two independent sources and prefer originals such as official data, standards or the actual paper.

faq.q: How can I tell if a citation from AI is real?
faq.a: Search for the exact title and authors in a library database, publisher site or Google Scholar, then open the item and confirm it says what the AI claimed. If you cannot find it, treat it as invented.

content:
To fact-check an AI answer, break it into individual claims, rank them by risk, trace each important claim to a reliable source, and record what you confirmed. Asking the AI "are you sure?" is not verification.

This matters for students, writers, marketers and professionals alike. A fluent paragraph can contain one wrong date or an invented study, and the error becomes yours the moment you reuse it.

## Step 1: Split the answer into claims

Paragraphs hide facts inside smooth prose. Pull them out. You can do this by hand or with a prompt:

```
List every factual claim in the text below as a numbered list.
One claim per line. Include names, dates, numbers, quotes and cause-and-effect statements.
Do not add or evaluate anything yet.

Text:
[paste]
```

Now you have a checklist rather than a vague feeling that the text is probably right.

## Step 2: Rank claims by risk

You do not have time to verify everything equally, so prioritize. Check first:

- **Anything the work depends on:** the claim your argument or decision rests on.
- **Specific details:** numbers, dates, names, quotes, titles.
- **Surprising claims:** if it sounds too neat or too dramatic, check it.
- **High-stakes topics:** health, law, finance, safety.
- **Anything you will publish or submit.**

General background statements that are easy to confirm can come later.

## Step 3: Find a reliable source

Prefer sources close to the origin of the information.

- **Primary sources:** official statistics offices, laws and regulations, standards bodies, company filings, the original research paper.
- **Strong secondary sources:** textbooks, established reference works, reputable news organizations with corrections policies.
- **Weak sources:** anonymous blogs, content farms, social posts, and other AI-generated pages that may repeat the same error.

When a statement appears on many websites, check whether they all trace back to one origin. Repetition is not confirmation.

## Step 4: Check the specifics properly

### Numbers and dates

Look up the figure in the original table or report. Confirm the year, the unit and what exactly was measured. AI often blends figures from different years or definitions.

### Quotes

Search the exact wording in quotation marks. If you cannot find it in a reliable source, do not use it as a quote. Misattributed and invented quotes are common.

### Citations and studies

Locate the item in a library catalog, publisher site or scholarly search. Open it and confirm the authors, year and, importantly, that it supports the claim. Some citations are real but do not say what was claimed.

### Definitions and technical explanations

Compare against a textbook or official documentation. Models can mix up similar terms.

## Step 5: Use AI as an assistant, not the judge

AI can speed up the process without being the final authority.

```
Here are claims from a draft. For each, suggest:
- what kind of source would confirm it,
- a search phrase I could use,
- how likely the claim is to be outdated or contested.
Do not state whether the claims are true.
```

Notice the final line. You are borrowing the model's organizing ability while keeping the judgment for yourself. If your tool offers web search, open every link it gives and read the page. Do not trust a summary of a source in place of the source.

## Step 6: Record what you verified

Keep a simple log, especially for work others will rely on.

| Claim | Status | Source checked | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Founded in year X | Confirmed | Official site, archive page | Date matches |
| Quote attributed to Y | Not found | Searched 3 sources | Removed |
| Growth figure | Corrected | Annual report | Original said wrong year |

A log makes revision easy and protects you if someone asks where a fact came from.

## Step 7: Fix or remove, then re-read

Replace incorrect claims with verified ones, delete anything you cannot confirm, and re-read the whole piece. Corrections can break the logic of nearby sentences. If a main claim fails, the argument may need rebuilding, not just patching.

## Spotting red flags quickly

- Very precise numbers without a named source.
- A "study" with no authors, year or journal.
- Quotes with no stated origin.
- Confident answers about very recent events or obscure topics.
- Claims that perfectly support what you hoped to find.
- Sources that cannot be found anywhere.

## Fact-checking for students

Teachers and institutions increasingly expect verification and honest disclosure of AI use. Treat AI as a starting point for finding questions and search terms, then build your work on sources you have read. Never submit invented references or unverified claims.

## A worked example

Imagine an AI-written paragraph says: "A well-known 2015 report found that 63 percent of students prefer digital textbooks, according to a leading education institute." Treat each element as a claim to test.

1. **The report:** search for its title or issuing body. If nothing appears, the report may not exist.
2. **The year:** if the report exists, check the year in the original.
3. **The figure:** find 63 percent in the document itself, not in a blog quoting it.
4. **The wording:** see exactly who was surveyed and what "prefer" meant. A survey of 200 people at one university does not support "students" in general.
5. **The attribution:** confirm the institute actually published it.

In practice, claims like this often turn out to be a distorted version of a real finding, or entirely invented. The point of checking is not to catch the AI out but to make sure that what you publish is true.

## Building a fast verification habit

For everyday work you need a lightweight routine, not a research project. Before using any AI-written fact, ask three questions: Could this be checked in under two minutes? Would it matter if it were wrong? Is it the sort of detail models often get wrong? If the answers are yes, yes and yes, check it now. For recurring work, keep a short list of trusted sources, such as official statistics sites, your library database and primary documentation, so verification starts from places you already trust instead of a blank search page.

## Common mistakes

- **Asking the AI to confirm itself.** It can reaffirm an error with the same confidence.
- **Checking only the easy claims.** The risky detail is often the one you skipped.
- **Trusting a source because it exists.** Quality and independence matter.
- **Not opening links.** A link or citation that looks right may not support the claim.
- **Stopping at the first search result.** Cross-check important facts.
- **Not keeping notes.** You will forget what you verified.

## Next steps

Learn more about [reducing hallucinations](/blog) in your prompts, use the [study planner](/study-planner) to schedule research time, or browse research prompts in the [student collection](/prompts/category/students).

title: How to Evaluate AI Answer Quality With a Simple Rubric
excerpt: Stop judging AI output by gut feeling. Use a simple rubric for accuracy, relevance, clarity and completeness to compare answers and improve your prompts.
seo_title: Evaluate AI Answer Quality With a Simple Rubric
seo_description: Judge AI answers consistently with a simple rubric covering accuracy, relevance, completeness, clarity and usability. Includes a scoring template and prompt.

faq.q: What makes an AI answer good?
faq.a: A good answer is accurate, relevant to your actual question, complete enough for your purpose, clearly written, and usable in the format you need. Which criteria matter most depends on the task you are doing.

faq.q: Can AI grade its own answers?
faq.a: It can offer a useful critique when given a rubric, but self-scores tend to be generous and it can miss its own errors. Use AI grading as a second opinion and make the final call yourself.

faq.q: How many criteria should a rubric have?
faq.a: Four to six criteria is enough. More than that slows you down and blurs priorities. Choose the criteria that matter for the task, and weight the most important ones higher.

faq.q: How do I compare answers from different AI tools?
faq.a: Give each tool the identical prompt, hide which tool wrote which answer if you can, and score every answer against the same rubric. Repeat with a few different prompts before drawing conclusions.

content:
To judge AI answers consistently, score them against a short rubric: accuracy, relevance, completeness, clarity and usability. Scoring takes a minute, removes the "it sounds good" bias, and shows you which part of your prompt to fix.

Without criteria, evaluation drifts toward style. Polished, confident answers feel better than they are. A rubric forces you to ask what you actually need.

## Why evaluate at all

You will use AI repeatedly for similar tasks, such as summaries, emails or explanations. Evaluating a few outputs carefully tells you:

- whether a prompt is good enough to reuse,
- which tool or setting suits a task,
- where errors tend to appear,
- when output needs human review before use.

It also builds the habit of reading critically rather than copying.

## A five-criterion rubric

Score each criterion from 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent).

| Criterion | Question to ask |
|---|---|
| Accuracy | Are the facts, numbers and reasoning correct? |
| Relevance | Does it answer what I actually asked, not a nearby question? |
| Completeness | Does it cover what I need, with nothing important missing? |
| Clarity | Is it well organized and easy to follow for the intended reader? |
| Usability | Can I use it as is, in the right format, tone and length? |

Add or swap criteria for special tasks. For creative writing, add originality and voice. For code, add correctness and readability. For study material, add alignment with your syllabus.

## Weighting for the task

Not all criteria matter equally. A research summary should weight accuracy heavily. A brainstorm should weight originality over polish. Decide weights before you read the answer, so the answer cannot persuade you that its strengths are the important ones.

A simple method: give accuracy a double score for factual tasks, or relevance a double score when you suspect the model drifts off topic.

## How to score accurately

### Check accuracy against something

You cannot score accuracy by reading alone. Verify at least the key claims using the process in our [fact-checking guide](/blog). If you did not check, write "unverified" rather than giving a high score.

### Compare with the prompt

Re-read your original request. Highlight every requirement: length, format, audience, constraints. Mark which were met. Missed constraints reveal prompt problems or model limits.

### Read as the intended reader

Imagine the person who will use the output. Would a beginner understand it? Would a busy manager find the key point in the first two lines?

## Using AI as a second reviewer

You can request a structured critique, then compare it with your own scores.

```
Evaluate the answer below against this rubric.
Score 1-5 for accuracy, relevance, completeness, clarity, usability.
For each score, give one sentence of evidence from the answer.
List the three most important weaknesses and suggest a better prompt to fix them.
Be critical. Do not praise unless justified.

My original request:
[paste]

The answer:
[paste]
```

Models tend to be lenient graders, so the instruction to be critical helps. Treat the scores as a prompt for your own thinking, not as measurements.

## Comparing two prompts or two tools

For a fair comparison:

1. Use the identical task and identical input.
2. Generate two or three outputs from each version.
3. Remove labels so you do not know which is which, if practical.
4. Score all outputs on the same rubric.
5. Note patterns, not single results. One output can be lucky.

Results vary from run to run, so a single comparison tells you little. Repeat with different tasks to see consistent differences.

## Turning scores into prompt improvements

Low scores point to specific fixes.

- **Low accuracy:** supply source text, narrow the scope, require evidence.
- **Low relevance:** restate the goal and audience, add an example of what you want.
- **Low completeness:** list the required points explicitly.
- **Low clarity:** specify structure, such as headings, bullets or a table.
- **Low usability:** state format, length and tone precisely.

Change one thing at a time, then run it again. If you change five things, you will not know which one helped.

## Keep a quality log

A simple spreadsheet with columns for date, task, prompt version, scores and notes becomes useful quickly. It shows which saved prompts deserve a place in your [prompt library](/blog) and which need rewriting.

## Know when AI output needs a human expert

Some tasks should never rest on a rubric score alone: medical, legal, financial, safety-critical or grading decisions. In these areas, a qualified person should review the result, and AI should support rather than decide.

## Worked example: scoring a study explanation

A student asks an AI to explain how vaccines train the immune system, for a 14-year-old. The answer reads well. Scoring against the rubric tells a more complete story. Accuracy: the student checks it against a textbook and finds it accurate, so 4 of 5 with one oversimplification. Relevance: it answers the question, 5. Completeness: it omits how memory cells work, 3. Clarity: good analogies, 5. Usability: the vocabulary is slightly above the target age, 3.

The total shows an answer that looks strong but fails the audience requirement. The next prompt targets precisely that: "Rewrite for a 14-year-old; avoid terms like antigen unless explained; add two sentences on memory cells." The rubric turned a vague "it's good" into a specific fix.

## Scoring different kinds of tasks

Adapt the rubric to the output type. For code, replace clarity with correctness and test it by running it. For brainstorming, score originality and variety, not polish. For emails, score whether the request is unmistakable in the first two sentences. For study material, score alignment with your syllabus. Keep the number of criteria small so scoring never becomes the main task. If a rubric takes longer than the work itself, simplify it until you actually use it.

## A quick evaluation checklist

When you have only a minute, run this short version. Did the answer address my exact question? Did I verify at least one important claim? Is anything missing that I expected? Would my intended reader understand it without help? Can I use it with minimal editing? If two or more answers are no, adjust the prompt and try again instead of patching the output by hand.

## Common mistakes

- **Judging by fluency.** Well-written errors are still errors.
- **Scoring without checking facts.** Accuracy needs verification.
- **Changing the rubric after seeing the answer.** Decide criteria first.
- **Evaluating one sample.** Outputs vary; test more than once.
- **Letting AI grade its own work uncritically.** Treat it as a second opinion.
- **Ignoring the reader.** Quality depends on who will use the answer.

## Next steps

Build better prompts with the [prompt builder](/prompt-builder), save high-scoring prompts from the [prompt library](/prompts), and compare options in our [AI tools directory](/ai-tools).

title: Privacy-Safe Prompting: How to Use AI Without Oversharing
excerpt: Learn what not to paste into an AI chat and how to anonymize text, use placeholders and check tool settings so you get help without exposing personal data.
seo_title: Privacy-Safe Prompting: Use AI Without Oversharing
seo_description: Protect yourself when using AI: learn what not to paste, how to anonymize text with placeholders, review privacy settings and build safer prompting habits.

faq.q: What should I never paste into an AI chatbot?
faq.a: Avoid passwords, financial account numbers, government ID numbers, private health details, confidential business or client information, and other people's personal data. If you would not post it publicly, think twice before pasting it.

faq.q: How do I anonymize text before using AI?
faq.a: Replace names, emails, phone numbers, addresses and company names with neutral placeholders such as [Person A] or [Client]. Remove identifying details like unique job titles or dates, and keep a private key so you can restore them afterward.

faq.q: Does AI keep my conversations?
faq.a: It depends on the tool, plan and your settings. Some services may retain chats or use them to improve products unless you opt out. Always read the official privacy policy and settings for the specific tool you use.

faq.q: Is it safe to use AI for work documents?
faq.a: Only if your employer permits it and the tool meets your organization's security rules. Use approved tools, follow company policy, and remove confidential details whenever you are unsure about the rules.

content:
The safest way to use AI is to share the minimum information needed: replace real names and identifiers with placeholders, never paste credentials or sensitive records, and check how your tool stores and uses conversations. You can still get strong results with anonymized text.

Many people paste emails, contracts, résumés or student data into chatbots without thinking about where the information goes. A few habits make that much safer.

## Know what you are sharing

When you type into an AI tool, the text is sent to a service run by a company. Depending on the product, plan and your settings, conversations might be stored, reviewed for safety or quality, or used to improve the service. Policies differ and change, so read the privacy policy and settings of the tool you use, rather than assuming.

A useful rule: treat a public chat tool like a conversation in a busy cafe. Fine for general questions, not for secrets.

## What not to paste

Avoid putting these into general-purpose AI tools:

- **Credentials:** passwords, API keys, recovery codes, private keys.
- **Financial details:** card numbers, bank account details, tax identifiers.
- **Government ID numbers** and similar identifiers.
- **Health information** about yourself or others, unless you fully understand the tool's handling and your own risk tolerance.
- **Confidential work material:** unreleased products, client records, internal strategy, legal matters.
- **Other people's personal data:** names with contact details, student records, employee reviews, private messages.
- **Anything covered by a confidentiality agreement.**

If an approved enterprise tool exists at your workplace, follow its rules. Even then, apply data minimization: share only what the task needs.

## The placeholder method

You rarely need real identifiers to get useful help. Swap them out.

| Real data | Placeholder |
|---|---|
| Sam Rivera | [Employee A] |
| Acme Holdings | [Company X] |
| sam@example.com | [email] |
| 12 Main Street | [address] |
| Order #48291 | [order number] |

Then prompt as usual. When the answer returns, you replace placeholders with real details yourself.

```
The text below has been anonymized. Placeholders in square brackets stand for real
details I will fill in later. Do not try to guess what they represent.
Rewrite the message to be more polite and concise. Keep all placeholders unchanged.

[anonymized text]
```

## Go beyond names

De-identification is not only removing names. Combinations of details can identify someone: a rare job title plus a city plus a date. Generalize where possible, for example "a manager at a mid-sized company" instead of a precise description. Remove metadata, file names and signature blocks that carry hidden details.

## Describe, do not paste

Often you can ask for help without sharing the document at all. Instead of pasting a private contract, describe the situation: "I am reviewing a services agreement. What clauses should I ask a lawyer about?" Instead of sharing a student's essay, ask for a general feedback rubric. This is especially useful for sensitive topics.

## Check tool settings

Take five minutes with each tool you use regularly.

1. Find the privacy or data controls in the settings.
2. Look for options about chat history and whether conversations are used to improve the product.
3. Check whether there is a temporary or incognito-style mode.
4. Learn how to delete conversations and what deletion actually covers.
5. Check what happens when you upload files or connect other apps.
6. Note whether your work or school provides a different, managed version.

Names and options vary by product and change over time, so rely on the official help pages rather than guesswork.

## Think about the output too

AI responses can contain mistakes about people, such as invented biographical details. Do not repeat claims about real individuals without verification, and avoid generating content that targets or misrepresents private persons. If you are drafting something about a named person, check every statement yourself.

## Safe habits for students and teachers

- Teachers should not paste student names, grades or identifying work into public tools unless school policy and the tool's terms allow it.
- Students should avoid sharing classmates' information or personal circumstances.
- Both should follow school and local data protection rules, which vary by country and institution.

## A quick pre-send checklist

- Does this contain names, contact details or identifiers I can remove?
- Is any of it confidential or covered by an agreement?
- Do I need the full text, or would a description work?
- Am I using an approved tool for this kind of data?
- Do I know the retention and training settings?

## Worked example: asking for help with a difficult email

Suppose you need to reply to a complaint from a customer. The unsafe route is to paste the complaint with the customer's name, order number, address and phone number. The safe route keeps the situation and removes identifiers: "A customer wrote that a delivery arrived late and damaged. They want a refund. Our policy allows refunds within a set period, and this request is inside it. Draft a polite reply that apologizes, confirms the refund process and asks them to reply with their order number through our normal support channel."

The reply is just as useful, and the sensitive details never left your control. You add the name and order number yourself afterward, in your own email program.

## Special care with children, health and employment

Some information carries higher risk or legal duties. Details about children and students deserve extra caution, and many places have specific rules about them. Health information is similarly sensitive. Employment matters such as performance reviews, disciplinary cases and salary details can harm real people if exposed or mishandled. In these areas, use descriptions and placeholders, follow your organization's policy, and ask your data protection or IT contact if you are unsure which tools are approved. When in doubt, leave it out.

## What to do if you shared too much

If you realize you pasted something sensitive, act promptly. Delete the conversation if the tool allows it, and check whether your settings allow deletion of stored data. If the information was a password or key, change it immediately. If it involved a client, student or colleague, tell the relevant person, such as your manager or data protection contact, as your organization's policy may require. Then update your habits and templates so that the same mistake is harder to repeat.

## Common mistakes

- **Pasting first, thinking later.** Once sent, you cannot take it back reliably.
- **Assuming private means private.** A chat window is not a secure vault.
- **Forgetting indirect identifiers.** Context can reveal who someone is.
- **Using personal accounts for work data.** This may violate policy.
- **Trusting placeholders blindly.** Check the text for names hiding in the middle of paragraphs.
- **Not reading settings.** Controls exist, but you must find them.

## Next steps

Create safer templates with the [prompt builder](/prompt-builder), see careers-related prompts that avoid oversharing in the [careers collection](/prompts/category/careers), or build a résumé offline with the [resume builder](/resume-builder).

title: How to Build a Personal Prompt Library You Will Actually Use
excerpt: Stop rewriting the same prompts. Learn how to collect, organize, version and improve your best prompts in a personal library that saves time every week.
seo_title: How to Build a Personal Prompt Library That Works
seo_description: Build a personal prompt library: choose a tool, organize by task, use variables, track versions and notes, and keep your best prompts easy to find and reuse.

faq.q: Where should I store my prompts?
faq.a: Use whatever you already open daily: a notes app, a document, a spreadsheet or a text-expander tool. The best system is the one you will actually use, so favor easy search and quick copy over fancy features.

faq.q: How many prompts should be in my library?
faq.a: Start with five to ten that you use repeatedly. A small, trusted collection beats hundreds of untested ones. Add a prompt only after it has worked well at least twice.

faq.q: How do I organize a prompt library?
faq.a: Group by task, such as summarize, rewrite, plan or analyze, rather than by tool. Use clear titles, a few tags and a short note about when to use each prompt and what to check in the output.

faq.q: Should I update old prompts?
faq.a: Yes. Review them occasionally, since tools and your needs change. Keep a version note for what changed and why, so you can return to an earlier version if the new one performs worse.

content:
A personal prompt library is a small, organized collection of prompts you have tested and can reuse. To build one, save only prompts that worked, give each a clear title and variables for the parts that change, and add a note about what to check in the output. Ten good prompts beat a hundred forgotten ones.

If you find yourself retyping the same instructions or searching old chats for "that prompt that worked," a library will pay for itself within a week.

## Why keep a library

- **Time:** you stop rebuilding instructions from memory.
- **Consistency:** the same task gets the same quality of instructions each time.
- **Learning:** seeing your prompts side by side shows what makes them work.
- **Sharing:** a tidy prompt is easy to hand to a teammate or classmate.

## Step 1: Choose a home that fits your habits

The tool matters less than the habit. Options:

- A notes app with search and tags.
- A single document with a table of contents.
- A spreadsheet with columns for title, task, prompt, notes and last used.
- A text-expander or snippet tool for instant pasting.
- A folder of plain text files, if you like simple systems.

Pick the place you already open every day. A fancy system you forget is worse than a plain document you use.

## Step 2: Save only what has earned a place

Do not save every prompt. Use a simple gate: a prompt enters the library after it has produced a good result at least twice, or once on a task that matters. This keeps the library trustworthy. When you open it, you know every entry has been tested.

## Step 3: Use a consistent entry format

A consistent format makes scanning fast.

```
TITLE: Summarize an article for revision
TASK TYPE: Summarize
```
