```
USE WHEN: I have a reading and need quick revision notes
PROMPT:
Summarize the text below for a student reviewing for an exam.
Output: 5 bullet points + 3 key terms with one-line definitions.
Use only the text. Mark anything unclear as "unclear in source."
Text: [PASTE TEXT]
CHECK: Compare key terms with the original; verify numbers.
VERSION: v2 (added "unclear in source" rule)
LAST USED: [date]
```

The **CHECK** line is easy to skip and very valuable. It reminds you what to verify, which supports responsible use.

## Step 4: Turn variable parts into placeholders

Good library prompts are templates. Mark the parts that change with capital letters in brackets, such as [TOPIC], [AUDIENCE], [WORD LIMIT] and [PASTE TEXT]. Keep placeholders consistent across prompts, so you always know where to type. Fixed parts, such as format rules and quality constraints, stay locked in.

## Step 5: Organize by task, not by tool

Tools change. Tasks do not. Useful categories include:

- Summarize and condense
- Rewrite and edit
- Plan and schedule
- Brainstorm
- Explain and teach
- Analyze and compare
- Extract and organize data
- Check and critique

Add two or three tags for subject or audience, such as "email" or "biology," so search works from several angles.

## Step 6: Version, do not overwrite

When you improve a prompt, save the new version and keep a one-line note about what changed. If the new version is worse on a different input, you can go back. Even a simple "v1, v2, v3" label with a reason is enough.

Test improvements on at least two different inputs. A prompt that works on one sample may fail on another.

## Step 7: Build a starter set

Begin with templates for the tasks you do every week. Examples that suit almost everyone:

1. A summary template with audience, length and priorities.
2. An editing template that lists changes instead of rewriting.
3. A brainstorming template with constraints.
4. A "critique my draft" template.
5. A plan builder for a goal with a deadline.
6. A checker that lists claims needing verification.

You can adapt ready-made options from the [prompt library](/prompts) and tweak them to your voice.

## Step 8: Review monthly

Set a short recurring reminder. Delete prompts you have not used, merge near-duplicates, and refine the ones you use most. Add notes about failures: "gives too long answers; add a word limit." These notes are where the learning happens.

## Keep privacy in mind

Your library should never contain passwords, private client data, student details or other sensitive information inside the examples. Store templates with placeholders, and keep real data out. See our guide on [privacy-safe prompting](/blog).

## Sharing with others

If you work in a team or class, agree on a shared format and a place to keep it. Add the owner and last review date to each entry so stale prompts are visible. Credit the people who contributed improvements.

## Worked example: a one-week starter library

On Monday, list the five tasks you repeat most, such as summarizing readings, drafting emails, planning your week, explaining difficult topics and checking drafts. On Tuesday and Wednesday, write one prompt for each using the entry format above. On Thursday, run each on two real inputs and note failures. On Friday, fix the weak ones, add the CHECK lines and save the final versions.

By the end of the week you will have five prompts you trust, with notes about their weaknesses. That is more useful than a folder of fifty untested snippets, and it gives you a base to grow from: each time a new task recurs a third time, it earns a template.

## Handling prompts that depend on context

Some prompts only work with background, such as your course, your writing style or your company's tone. Keep a separate "context block" in the library that you paste at the start of a chat: a few lines describing your role, level, preferences and rules like "ask me questions if my request is unclear." Keeping context separate stops every template from becoming long, and you can swap context blocks when your situation changes, for example from one course to another or from work to personal use.

## A quick library health check

Once a quarter, ask four questions. Which five prompts do I use most, and are they in good shape? Which prompts have I not touched in months and can I archive them? Which tasks do I still write from scratch that deserve a template? Which entries lack a CHECK line? A short review keeps the library lean and keeps it matching how you actually work today.

## Common mistakes

- **Saving everything.** A cluttered library is a library you stop using.
- **No placeholders.** Prompts with fixed details need rewriting every time.
- **No notes on checking.** Reuse without verification invites errors.
- **Organizing by tool.** Tasks stay stable while tools change.
- **Never reviewing.** Old prompts quietly stop working well.
- **Overwriting versions.** You lose the ability to compare.

## Next steps

Start your collection with prompts from the [productivity category](/prompts/category/productivity), customize them in the [prompt builder](/prompt-builder), and explore the full [prompt library](/prompts) for more templates.

title: Prompt Debugging: How to Fix Bad AI Responses Fast
excerpt: When an AI answer misses the mark, diagnose the prompt, not just the model. Use a step-by-step debugging method to find the cause and fix it with one change.
seo_title: Prompt Debugging: Fix Bad AI Responses Fast
seo_description: Learn prompt debugging: diagnose why an AI response failed, isolate the cause, change one variable at a time and test fixes. Includes a symptom-to-fix table.

faq.q: Why is my AI prompt not working?
faq.a: Common causes are missing context, a vague goal, conflicting instructions, no format specified, or too many tasks in one prompt. Compare the output with what you wanted, identify the gap, and fix the prompt part that should have prevented it.

faq.q: Should I start a new chat when answers go wrong?
faq.a: Often yes. Long conversations can accumulate confusing instructions or drift off the goal. Start fresh with a clean, improved prompt that includes everything needed, rather than patching a messy thread.

faq.q: How do I get AI to follow my instructions exactly?
faq.a: Often yes. Long conversations can accumulate confusing instructions or drift away from the goal. Start fresh with a clean, improved prompt that includes everything needed, rather than patching a messy thread.

faq.q: Is it better to rewrite a prompt or add follow-ups?
faq.a: Use follow-ups for small adjustments. When the output is wrong in a fundamental way, rewrite the original prompt, because the misunderstanding may be baked in. Save the version that works.

content:
To debug a prompt, compare the output with what you wanted, name the specific gap, trace it to a missing or conflicting part of the prompt, then change one thing and test again. Treat it like fixing code: isolate, change, retest.

Most "bad AI answers" are not random. They have causes you can find. This guide gives a repeatable method and a table of common symptoms and fixes.

## Step 1: Describe the failure precisely

"It's bad" cannot be fixed. Write one sentence naming the gap:

- "The answer is too long and generic."
- "It ignored my word limit."
- "It invented a statistic."
- "The tone is too formal for my audience."
- "It answered a different question."

Precision points straight to the part of the prompt that needs work.

## Step 2: Re-read your own prompt as a stranger

Read the prompt as if you knew nothing about your situation. Ask:

- Is the goal stated, or only the topic?
- Is the audience clear?
- Are the constraints (length, format, tone) written down, or only in my head?
- Are there two instructions that conflict, such as "be brief" and "cover everything in detail"?
- Did I ask for several different tasks in one message?

Many failures vanish when you notice that the key information was never in the prompt.

## Step 3: Match the symptom to a likely cause

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Generic, bland output | No audience, purpose or specifics | Add who it is for, why, and concrete details |
| Wrong format | Format not specified | State exact structure, with a short example |
| Too long or too short | No length limit | Give an exact limit |
| Ignores a rule | Rule buried in a long prompt or contradicted | Move to a clear numbered list, remove conflicts |
| Invented facts | Asked from memory with no source | Supply source text, allow "not found" |
| Wrong tone | Tone described vaguely | Name the reader and give a sample sentence |
| Answers a different question | Ambiguous wording | Rephrase, add what is out of scope |
| Shallow reasoning | Task too big in one step | Split into steps or ask to work through stages |
| Inconsistent results | Underspecified task | Add criteria and an example |

## Step 4: Change one thing at a time

If you rewrite everything, you will not learn which change helped. Alter one variable, run the prompt again, and compare. Because outputs vary between runs, test two or three times before deciding.

A simple log helps:

```
Version: v3
Change: added "Maximum 120 words" and an example sentence
Result: length fixed, tone still too formal
Next: add audience description
```

## Step 5: Use the model to help diagnose

You can ask the model to critique the prompt itself.

```
Here is a prompt I used, and the response I got.
What I wanted instead: [describe]

1. Point out ambiguities or missing information in my prompt.
2. List any instructions that may have conflicted.
3. Rewrite my prompt to fix those issues without changing my goal.
4. Briefly explain each change.

Prompt: [paste]
Response: [paste]
```

Review its suggestions critically. It can spot ambiguity well, but it may also add unnecessary complexity. Keep only the changes that address your actual gap.

## Step 6: Add an example

When descriptions fail, show the target. One short example of the desired output often fixes format, tone and level of detail at once. Make the example clearly labeled and note that the model should match its style but not copy its content.

## Step 7: Simplify or split

If the prompt tries to do too much, the model may do each part poorly. Split it:

1. Ask for an outline first.
2. Approve or edit the outline.
3. Ask for the full draft section by section.

This also makes errors easier to locate, because each stage is small.

## Step 8: Reset the conversation when needed

Long chats can pile up earlier instructions, corrections and partial drafts. The model may weigh old text unexpectedly. If results get worse the longer you go, copy your best, clean prompt into a new conversation. Include any decisions made along the way, such as "avoid X, the audience is Y."

## Checklist for a stubborn prompt

- Is the goal in one clear sentence?
- Is the audience named?
- Are constraints explicit and consistent?
- Is the format described or shown?
- Is the necessary source material included?
- Is there only one main task?
- Have I tested it more than once?

## Debugging for different tasks

**Writing prompts** usually fail on tone and specificity. Add a reader, a purpose and details to include.

**Analysis prompts** fail on vague criteria. State what to compare and how to judge.

**Data prompts** fail on edge cases. Define columns, allowed values and what to do with missing information.

**Study prompts** fail when they ask for too much at once. Break topics into small sections and request practice questions.

## Worked example: from vague to fixed in three rounds

A job seeker asks: "Write a cover letter for a marketing job." The output is generic and full of clichés. Round one diagnosis: no role details, no experience, no tone. The fix adds the job description, three real achievements and a length limit. The result improves but sounds stiff. Round two diagnosis: tone is undefined. The fix adds "warm, confident, no phrases like passionate team player" and a sample sentence in the writer's own voice. Round three: one claim in the letter overstates an achievement. The fix is the writer's own edit, plus the rule "use only the achievements listed; do not add numbers."

Each round targeted one cause, and the final prompt went into the library as a template. You can build a similar letter structure with the [cover letter builder](/cover-letter-builder) and check the claims yourself.

## When the model is the limit, not the prompt

Sometimes a better prompt will not help. Models can struggle with exact counting, long arithmetic, very recent events and tasks needing access to files or sites they cannot see. If you have tried clear instructions, an example and a split into steps and the output is still wrong, change the approach. Do the calculation in a spreadsheet, supply the missing text, use a tool built for that task or do that portion by hand. Knowing when to stop tuning is part of debugging.

## Common mistakes

- **Blaming the tool first.** Often the prompt omitted key information.
- **Rewriting everything at once.** You lose the signal about what worked.
- **Adding more words instead of clearer ones.** Longer is not better; sharper is.
- **Repeating "be accurate" and "be detailed."** Structure helps more than adjectives.
- **Testing once.** A single good or bad output may be luck.
- **Not saving the fix.** Record the working version in your library.

## Next steps

Rebuild a stubborn request in the [prompt builder](/prompt-builder), compare patterns in the [prompt library](/prompts), and keep working versions in your [productivity prompts](/prompts/category/productivity) notes.

title: Multi-Step Prompt Workflows: A Practical Chaining Guide
excerpt: Break big tasks into a chain of small prompts. Learn how to design multi-step AI workflows with checkpoints, clear handoffs and human review between stages.
seo_title: Multi-Step Prompt Workflows: Prompt Chaining Guide
seo_description: Learn prompt chaining: split complex tasks into steps, pass outputs forward, add review checkpoints and build dependable multi-step AI workflows.

faq.q: What is prompt chaining?
faq.a: Prompt chaining means splitting a complex task into a sequence of smaller prompts, where the output of one step becomes the input of the next. It improves control and makes errors easier to find and fix.

faq.q: When should I use a multi-step workflow instead of one prompt?
faq.a: Use steps when a task has distinct stages, such as research, outline, draft and edit, or when one big prompt gives messy results. Simple tasks usually work fine in a single, clear prompt.

faq.q: Do I need coding skills to chain prompts?
faq.a: No. You can chain prompts manually in a normal chat by copying outputs forward. Coding or automation tools can run chains for you, but the design thinking is the same.

faq.q: How do I keep quality high across steps?
faq.a: Add a review checkpoint after each important step, pass only the necessary information forward, and fix errors before you move on. Mistakes in early stages carry into every later step.

content:
A multi-step prompt workflow splits a complex task into small stages, where each stage has one job and its output feeds the next. This usually beats a single giant prompt because each step is easier to specify, check and correct.

You can run a chain by hand in any chat tool by copying results forward. The skill is in designing the stages.

## Why one big prompt often fails

When you ask for research, structure, drafting, editing and formatting in a single request, the model must juggle many goals. Typical results: skipped requirements, shallow sections and errors you cannot locate. Chaining helps because:

- each step has a narrow, testable goal,
- you can review and correct between steps,
- you can reuse good steps in other workflows,
- mistakes do not silently compound.

## The basic design pattern

1. **Define the final deliverable** and who it is for.
2. **List the stages** needed to get there.
3. **Write one prompt per stage** with a clear input and a clear output.
4. **Insert checkpoints** where you review before continuing.
5. **Save the chain** as a reusable template.

## Example: from topic to a finished study guide

Suppose a student has class notes and wants a study guide.

### Step 1: Clean and structure the notes

```
Below are my raw class notes. Reorganize them into headings and bullet points.
Do not add information that is not in the notes. If something seems incomplete, mark it [unclear].
Notes: [paste]
```

Checkpoint: skim the result, fix marked gaps using your textbook.

### Step 2: Extract key terms

```
From the organized notes below, list key terms with a one-line definition each,
using only the notes. Flag any definition you are unsure about.
```

Checkpoint: compare the definitions with your course materials.

### Step 3: Create practice questions

```
Using the notes and terms, write 10 practice questions: 6 recall, 4 application.
Provide an answer key that cites which note section supports each answer.
```

Checkpoint: answer them yourself first, then check the key.

### Step 4: Build a revision plan

```
I have [number] days before the exam and [hours] per day.
Create a revision schedule using the topics above. Include review sessions.
```

Notice that no single step is difficult, and every step can be verified. You could also build the schedule with the [study planner](/study-planner).

## Designing good handoffs

The output of one stage becomes the input of the next, so make it clean.

- **Specify output format.** If step 2 will read step 1's output, ask for a consistent structure like a numbered list or table.
- **Pass only what is needed.** Pasting everything every time creates clutter and can cause confusion.
- **Carry key constraints forward.** Restate audience, tone or length in later steps, since the model may not weigh earlier ones.
- **Label inputs.** Use headings such as "Outline:" and "Draft:" so the model knows which is which.

## Where to place checkpoints

Checkpoints are the main advantage of manual chains. Add one:

- after any step that generates facts,
- after structure decisions, such as an outline,
- before any step that is costly to redo,
- before sharing or submitting anything.

At a checkpoint, you may fix the output by hand, ask for a revision, or restart the step with a better prompt.

## Common chain patterns

### Research to draft

1. List questions to answer.
2. Gather and verify facts yourself from sources.
3. Outline using only verified facts.
4. Draft section by section.
5. Edit for clarity and tone.
6. Final fact check.

### Decision support

1. Define criteria and weights.
2. List options with pros and cons from provided information.
3. Score options in a table.
4. Ask for the strongest case against the top choice.
5. Decide yourself.

### Content repurposing

1. Summarize the source.
2. Extract the three main ideas.
3. Draft one format, such as a newsletter.
4. Adapt to another format, such as a short script.
5. Review for consistency.

## A reusable chain template

```
GOAL: [final deliverable + audience]
STEP 1 (input: raw material -> output: structured version)
STEP 2 (input: step 1 -> output: key points)
STEP 3 (input: step 2 + constraints -> output: draft)
STEP 4 (input: draft -> output: critique list)
STEP 5 (input: draft + critique -> output: revised draft)
CHECKPOINTS: after 1, 3 and 5
```

Adapt the number of steps. Three to five is enough for most tasks. More stages add overhead without much benefit.

## Add a critic stage

A strong habit is to include a step where the model reviews work it produced earlier.

```
Act as a critical reviewer. Read the draft below against the original goal.
List missing points, weak arguments, unsupported claims and unclear sentences.
Do not rewrite yet.
```

Then feed the critique into a revision step. Keep your own judgment in the loop, because a model critique can miss errors or suggest unnecessary changes.

## Managing context in long chats

Long conversations can drift. If a chain goes beyond a handful of steps, start a new chat with a short "state summary": goal, decisions made, current draft. This resets confusion and keeps the model focused.

## Worked example: a job application chain

A job seeker can use a chain with checkpoints. Step one: paste the job description and ask for a list of the top eight requirements in a table with the exact phrases used. Step two: paste your own verified experience and ask which requirements it covers, which are partly covered and which are gaps, using only what you provided. Step three: ask for suggestions of truthful ways to phrase relevant experience, without inventing achievements. Step four: draft résumé bullet points yourself, then ask for a critique. Step five: do a final proofreading pass.

Checkpoints sit after steps two and four, because those are the places where invented claims could slip in. Tools like the [resume builder](/resume-builder) and [ATS resume checker](/ats-resume-checker) fit naturally at the end of the chain.

## Recovering when a chain goes wrong

When a final output is poor, trace backward. Was the last prompt unclear, or did the input already contain an error? Check each stage's output in reverse order until you find the first bad one, fix it and rerun everything after it. Keeping each stage's output in a document, labeled by step, makes this easy. You will often find that the problem began two steps earlier than it appeared, which is exactly why short stages with checkpoints are worth the extra minutes.

## Common mistakes

- **Making steps too large.** A step with several jobs defeats the purpose.
- **Skipping checkpoints.** Early errors spread through the chain.
- **Passing unverified facts forward.** Verify before building on them.
- **Forgetting constraints in later steps.** Restate tone, length and audience.
- **Over-engineering.** Simple tasks do not need five stages.
- **Not saving the chain.** A tested workflow deserves a place in your [prompt library](/blog).

## Next steps

Plan your own sequence in the [prompt builder](/prompt-builder), adapt templates from the [productivity prompts](/prompts/category/productivity), or browse supporting [AI tools](/ai-tools).

title: AI Image Prompt Basics: How to Describe What You Want
excerpt: Learn the building blocks of a good AI image prompt: subject, style, composition, lighting and constraints, with examples and a template for beginners.
seo_title: AI Image Prompt Basics for Beginners
seo_description: Learn AI image prompt basics: describe subject, style, composition, lighting and mood, refine step by step, avoid common mistakes. Template included.

faq.q: What makes a good AI image prompt?
faq.a: A good image prompt names the subject, the setting, the style or medium, the composition, lighting and mood, and any constraints. Clear, concrete descriptions beat long lists of vague adjectives.

faq.q: How long should an image prompt be?
faq.a: Often one to three descriptive sentences is enough to start. Add detail where results are wrong, rather than writing a huge prompt first. Different tools handle length differently, so check the tool's own guidance.

faq.q: Why do AI images have strange hands or text?
faq.a: Many image models struggle with fine structure such as hands, small details and legible text. Simplify the scene, choose compositions that hide difficult areas, or add text later in an editor.

faq.q: Can I use AI-generated images commercially?
faq.a: It depends on the tool's terms, your plan and local law, which differ and change. Read the official terms for the specific tool, avoid copying living artists' styles or protected characters, and get advice for important commercial use.

content:
A good AI image prompt describes the subject, setting, style, composition, lighting and mood in plain, concrete language. Start with a short description, look at the result, then add or change one detail at a time until the image matches your idea.

Image tools differ in features and wording rules, so check the official guide for yours. The basics below apply to most text-to-image tools.

## The building blocks of an image prompt

### 1. Subject

What is the main thing in the picture? Be specific. "A dog" is vague. "A small brown terrier wearing a yellow raincoat" is clear. Mention number, age, clothing, pose and action if they matter.

### 2. Setting

Where is it happening? "On a quiet wet street at dusk" gives the model a world to build. Add time of day, season, indoor or outdoor and background details.

### 3. Style or medium

Say how the image should look: photograph, flat vector illustration, watercolor, pencil sketch, 3D render, paper cut-out, isometric diagram. This choice changes everything, so name it early.

### 4. Composition

Describe framing and viewpoint: close-up portrait, wide shot, top-down view, low angle, centered subject with empty space for text. If the image will be a slide or banner, say so.

### 5. Lighting and color

Light shapes mood. Try soft morning light, warm sunset glow, dramatic side lighting or flat even lighting. For color, name a palette: muted earth tones, bright primary colors, pastel blues and pinks.

### 6. Mood

One or two mood words guide the overall feel: calm, playful, mysterious, professional, nostalgic.

## A beginner template

```
[Style/medium] of [specific subject doing action] in [setting],
[composition/viewpoint], [lighting], [color palette], [mood].
No text, no watermark.
```

Example:

```
Flat vector illustration of a student studying at a desk with a stack of books
and a small plant, side view, soft warm lamp light, muted green and cream palette,
calm and focused mood. Simple shapes, plenty of empty space, no text.
```

## Be concrete, not decorative

Piling on adjectives like "beautiful, stunning, amazing, masterpiece" adds little. Concrete visual information gives the model something to use. Compare:

- Weak: "A beautiful amazing landscape."
- Better: "A wide mountain valley at sunrise, low mist over a river, pine forest in the foreground, soft golden light."

## Refine in small steps

Treat the first image as a draft.

1. Generate a first version from a short prompt.
2. Note what is wrong: style, framing, colors, extra objects.
3. Change one thing in the prompt.
4. Regenerate and compare.
5. Keep a note of the version that worked.

If you change everything at once, you will not know what caused the improvement.

## Handling unwanted elements

You can often state what you do not want: "no text," "no people in the background," "plain background." Some tools have a separate field for exclusions, and some ignore negatives. Check how yours behaves, and when negatives fail, describe what you want instead. "An empty street" works better than "no cars."

## Common trouble spots

- **Hands and small details:** may look distorted. Use poses where hands are out of view or simple.
- **Text inside images:** often garbled. Generate the picture without text, then add words in a design tool.
- **Counting objects:** models can miss exact numbers. Keep counts small or fix in editing.
- **Consistency across images:** characters may change between generations. Reuse the same detailed description and check tool features for consistency.
- **Complex scenes:** too many subjects compete. Simplify or build scenes in layers.

## Prompts for practical uses

### Study and teaching visuals

"Simple diagram-style illustration showing the water cycle, flat colors, labeled areas left blank, clean white background." Add labels yourself so they are accurate.

### Blog and presentation covers

"Minimal vector illustration of a laptop and notebook on a desk, pastel palette, wide composition with space at the left for a title." Ask for no text and add typography afterward.

### Social media and design drafts

Use generated images as mood boards or rough drafts, then refine in a design app.

## Responsible use

- **Copyright and style:** avoid prompts that copy a living artist's distinctive style or reproduce protected characters and logos.
- **People:** do not create deceptive images of real people or content meant to mislead.
- **Disclosure:** label AI-generated images where context or rules require it.
- **Terms of use:** commercial rights and restrictions vary by tool, so read the official terms.
- **Accuracy:** AI images of diagrams, maps or science often contain errors. Do not use them as factual references without checking.

## Worked example: iterating on one idea

Say you want a cover image for a blog post about time management. Attempt one: "A clock." The result is a plain photo-style clock. Attempt two adds style and setting: "Flat vector illustration of a desk with an alarm clock, a notebook and a cup of tea, top-down view." Better, but the colors are harsh. Attempt three adds palette and mood: "Soft pastel palette, calm mood, plenty of empty space on the right." Now the image works as a cover with room for a title.

Three short rounds, one change each, produced a usable result. Keep your final prompt in a notes file so you can reproduce the style for the next post and keep a consistent look across your content.

## Reading the result critically

When an image arrives, inspect it before using it. Zoom in on faces, hands, edges and background objects for strange artifacts. Check that signs, labels and diagrams contain no nonsense text. If the image is meant to teach, confirm that every depicted detail is correct, since a pretty but wrong diagram can mislead a learner. Finally, consider whether the image could be mistaken for a real photograph of a real event, and label it as AI-generated where that matters.

## A quick image prompt checklist

Before generating, ask yourself: Have I named the subject precisely? Have I chosen a medium or style? Do I know the shape and use of the image, such as a square icon or a wide banner? Have I said what to leave out? Afterward, inspect the result for artifacts, wrong details and anything that could mislead. Keep the prompt that worked, because a reliable recipe for your style saves a lot of time later.

## Common mistakes

- **Writing only adjectives.** Name concrete things.
- **Forgetting the style.** Without it, the tool chooses for you.
- **Overloading the prompt.** Too many ideas produce a muddle.
- **Changing many variables per attempt.** You cannot learn from that.
- **Relying on the image for facts.** Verify any educational content.
- **Ignoring the terms.** Rights and rules differ by service.

## Next steps

Draft text-based prompts in the [prompt builder](/prompt-builder), browse more creative ideas in the [prompt library](/prompts), or compare creative [AI tools](/ai-tools).

title: How to Summarize Research Papers With AI Responsibly
excerpt: Use AI to navigate dense research papers without skipping the reading. Prompts for structure, methods, limits and plain-language explanations, plus checks.
seo_title: Summarize Research Papers With AI Responsibly
seo_description: Use AI to understand research papers: prompts for structure, methods, findings and limits, plain-language explanations, and checks to keep reading honest.

faq.q: Can AI accurately summarize academic papers?
faq.a: It can give a useful overview, but it may misstate methods, results or limitations, especially with numbers and nuance. Use summaries to orient yourself, then read the abstract, methods and results of the original for anything you will cite.

faq.q: Is it okay to cite a paper I only read through an AI summary?
faq.a: No. Cite only what you have actually read and confirmed in the original. A summary can omit conditions or misreport findings, and citing it as if you read the paper is poor scholarship.

faq.q: What should I ask AI about a research paper?
faq.a: Ask for the research question, method, sample, main findings, limitations and how it relates to other work. Also ask for plain-language definitions of terms, and for questions you should ask while reading the original.

faq.q: How do I avoid plagiarism when using AI for research?
faq.a: Write your own notes and synthesis in your own words, cite original sources properly, and follow your institution's AI policy on assistance. Do not paste AI-generated text as your own analysis.

content:
Use AI to prepare for reading a research paper, not to replace it. Ask for the research question, method, findings and limitations from the text you supply, then read the original sections yourself and check every number you plan to use.

Dense papers are intimidating, and AI can lower the barrier by explaining jargon and structure. The risk is trusting a summary that quietly changes what the study actually found.

## What AI can and cannot do here

**Helpful for:**
- giving a structured overview before you read,
- explaining unfamiliar terms in plain language,
- generating questions to guide your reading,
- comparing the structure of several papers,
- helping you draft your own notes in a consistent format.

**Unreliable for:**
- exact figures, sample sizes and statistics,
- the strength and limits of evidence,
- details of methods,
- citations and references it generates from memory.

If you paste the paper text, accuracy improves because the model reads rather than recalls. If you do not, it may describe a paper it has never seen, which is a serious hallucination risk.

## Step 1: Read the abstract and conclusion first

Before using AI, read the abstract yourself. It gives you a baseline so you can recognize when a summary drifts. Skim the headings, figures and conclusion to get a feel for the structure.

## Step 2: Ask for a structured overview of supplied text

```
Below is the text of a research paper. Using ONLY this text, fill in:
1. Research question
2. Study design and method (in plain language)
3. Sample or data used
4. Main findings (include numbers exactly as written)
5. Limitations the authors state
6. What the authors conclude
If any item is not in the text, write "not stated."
Quote the sentence that supports each answer.

Text: [paste]
```

The "quote the sentence" instruction makes verification quick. If the quote does not support the summary line, correct it.

## Step 3: Get plain-language help with terms

When you hit jargon, ask for an explanation in context.

```
In the passage below, explain the terms "[term 1]" and "[term 2]" for a first-year
student. Give a simple analogy for each, then a one-line precise definition.
Passage: [paste]
```

Check specialized definitions in a textbook or glossary, since models sometimes blur similar terms.

## Step 4: Evaluate the study critically

AI can prompt your thinking, but the judgment is yours.

```
Based on the text, list questions I should ask about this study, such as:
- Is the sample appropriate for the claim?
- Does the method support the conclusion?
- What alternative explanations exist?
- What is not addressed?
Do not answer them; just give me the questions with a note on where in the paper to look.
```

Then look for the answers in the paper. This builds the skill of reading research critically, which is often the real learning objective.

## Step 5: Verify the key details

For anything you intend to use:

- Open the original and find the number, quote or claim.
- Confirm context: population, conditions, time period.
- Check that "significant" or "effective" means what the summary implies.
- Make sure the paper actually reports what the summary says, not what is commonly believed about the topic.

## Step 6: Take your own notes

Turn what you learned into notes in your own words. A useful template:

```
Citation: [full reference you have verified]
Question:
Method:
Key finding (with page number):
Limitations:
How it connects to my topic:
My questions:
```

Page numbers let you return and quote accurately. These notes are what you will draw on when writing, not the AI's text.

## Comparing several papers

Once you have verified summaries, a comparison table can help.

```
Here are my own notes on three papers. Create a table comparing them by
question, method, sample, main finding and limitation.
Then point out where the papers agree or disagree. Use only my notes.
```

Because the model uses your verified notes, errors from unsupported memory are less likely. You still need to read the table critically.

## Be careful with references

Models can produce references that look real but do not exist. Never copy a reference list from AI. Find each source in a library database or publisher site, confirm authors, year and title, and read enough of it to know what it says. If your tool can search the web or documents, open the sources yourself.

## Academic honesty

Check your institution's or journal's policy on AI use. Many allow limited support but expect disclosure, and none accept invented citations. Use AI for understanding and organizing, and do your own synthesis, argument and writing. Reading the papers you cite is not optional.

## Worked example: a three-paper reading session

A student has three papers to read for a seminar. They begin by reading each abstract themselves and noting the research question in a line. Next they paste each paper's text into the structured overview prompt and compare the AI output with their abstract notes. In one case the AI says the sample was "adults," but the paper says "university students," a difference that limits the conclusion. The mismatch sends the student back to the methods section, where they notice a limitation the authors discuss at length.

That small catch shows the right relationship with the tool. The summary pointed to where to look, and the student's reading corrected it. If the student had trusted the summary, the seminar discussion would have rested on a misstatement.

## Reading strategies AI can support

Papers are not meant to be read front to back. Use AI to plan a reading order: abstract, introduction's final paragraph, figures, results, then methods when needed. Ask it to generate a glossary of terms from the paper text and to suggest what background knowledge you might lack. Then, after reading, test yourself: explain the paper's contribution aloud without notes, and only afterwards compare with an AI-generated summary to see what you missed. Using it after, not before, reading often builds stronger understanding.

## A quick pre-citation checklist

Before citing a paper, confirm that you have read the relevant sections yourself, that the authors, year and title match a library or publisher record, that the claim you attribute to the paper appears in it, and that you represent its limits fairly. If any item is missing, do not cite it yet. This checklist protects you from the most common AI-related research errors and keeps your reference list honest.

## Common mistakes

- **Summarizing from memory.** Without the text, the model may fabricate a paper.
- **Skipping the original.** You cannot judge what the summary left out.
- **Copying numbers unverified.** Statistical details are easy to misreport.
- **Citing the summary.** Cite the paper, and only after reading it.
- **Letting AI do the critical thinking.** Evaluation is part of the work.
- **Using generated references.** Verify every one.

## Next steps

Plan your reading time with the [study planner](/study-planner), find research-friendly templates in the [student prompts](/prompts/category/students), and assemble a request in the [prompt builder](/prompt-builder).

title: Feedback Prompts: How to Ask AI to Critique Your Draft
excerpt: Get honest, specific feedback instead of empty praise. Use critique prompts with a reader, criteria and a ranked fix list to improve essays, emails and plans.
seo_title: Feedback Prompts: Ask AI to Critique Your Draft
seo_description: Get useful AI feedback on your draft: use critique prompts with a defined reader, criteria and ranked fixes, avoid flattery, and decide which advice to accept.

faq.q: Why does AI only say nice things about my writing?
faq.a: Models tend to be agreeable. Ask for a critical review, name specific criteria, and require the top weaknesses ranked by importance. Telling it not to praise unless justified also helps produce candid feedback.

faq.q: Should I let AI rewrite my draft after feedback?
faq.a: Usually revise it yourself using the feedback. If you do ask for a rewrite, treat it as an example, compare it with your version and keep your own voice. Follow any rules your school or employer sets.

faq.q: What criteria should I give for feedback?
faq.a: Use criteria that match the purpose: clarity of main point, structure, evidence, tone for the reader, and length. For an essay you might add alignment with the assignment rubric, which you should paste in.

faq.q: Can AI feedback replace a teacher or editor?
faq.a: No. It is quick and available anytime, but it lacks knowledge of your course, audience and context, and can be wrong. Use it for early drafts, then seek human feedback for important work.

content:
For useful AI feedback, tell the model who the reader is, what the piece should achieve and which criteria matter, then ask for the biggest problems first. Without those instructions, many tools respond with mild praise and a few cosmetic edits.

Critique prompts are one of the best uses of AI because you stay the author. The model points at weaknesses; you decide what to change.

## Why default feedback is weak

Models lean toward being agreeable and tidy. If you paste a draft and ask "thoughts?", you will often get a compliment, three generic suggestions and a polished rewrite you did not request. To get something better, you need to:

- define the reader and purpose,
- supply criteria,
- request ranked, specific, evidence-based comments,
- forbid rewriting until you ask.

## The anatomy of a critique prompt

1. **Role:** "Act as a critical editor / skeptical reader / exam marker."
2. **Context:** the audience and the goal of the piece.
3. **Criteria:** what to evaluate.
4. **Format:** how to present feedback.
5. **Limits:** no rewriting, no flattery.

```
Act as a critical but fair editor.
Reader: [who will read this]
Goal of the piece: [what it should achieve]

Review the draft below on: main point clarity, structure, evidence, tone for this
reader, and anything missing.

Format:
- One sentence stating what you think the main point is.
- The 3 most serious problems, ranked, each with a quote from the draft and why it matters.
- 3 smaller issues.
- 2 things that work well and should not change.
Do not rewrite the draft. Do not praise anything unless you can justify it.

Draft:
[paste]
```

The first item is a diagnostic: if the model's description of your main point differs from yours, readers will probably misread it too.

## Choose the reviewer persona that fits

Different readers notice different things.

- **Skeptical reader:** finds unsupported claims and leaps in logic.
- **Busy manager:** judges whether the key message is clear in the first lines.
- **Beginner:** flags jargon and missing steps.
- **Exam marker:** checks coverage against the stated rubric.
- **Hiring manager:** looks for relevance and concrete results in an application.

Run the same draft past two personas and compare. Conflicting advice shows you where the draft depends on the audience.

## Use your rubric

If you have an assignment brief, a job description or a style guide, paste the relevant part and ask for a check against it.

```
Here is the assignment brief. List each requirement and mark whether my draft
meets it: fully, partly or not at all. Quote the part of my draft that supports
your judgment. Do not suggest wording yet.
```

This catches missing requirements, which are a common reason for lost marks or rejected proposals.

## Ask for the argument map

For essays and reports, request a skeleton.

```
List the claims in my draft in order, with the evidence offered for each.
Mark any claim that has no evidence and any evidence that is not linked to a claim.
```

Seeing the structure laid bare is often more useful than line comments.

## Decide what advice to accept

AI feedback is advice, not a verdict. Triage it:

1. **Accept** points you agree with and can confirm by re-reading.
2. **Test** points you are unsure about: read the passage as a reader would.
3. **Reject** points that conflict with your purpose, style or the assignment rules.
4. **Verify** any factual correction before changing the text.

Keep a short note of what you changed and why. It helps in conversations with teachers or editors.

## Second round: targeted follow-ups

After the first critique, go deeper on one issue.

- "Show three different ways I could strengthen paragraph 4's evidence. Do not write the content for me."
- "Where does the pacing drag? Quote the sentences."
- "What question would a skeptical reader ask after paragraph 2?"

These keep you doing the writing while using the model as a sounding board.

## Feedback for different documents

- **Emails:** ask whether the request is clear in two sentences and whether the tone fits the recipient.
- **Résumés:** ask for gaps against a job description, then fix them with truthful details. Our [ATS resume checker](/ats-resume-checker) can complement this.
- **Presentations:** ask for the one message per slide and where the audience may get lost.
- **Study answers:** ask for a marker's view against the rubric, then compare with your teacher's feedback.

## Responsible use

Use feedback to improve work you create. Do not ask AI to write the whole piece and present it as your own where that is not allowed. Follow your school, publisher or employer rules about AI assistance and disclose use when required.

## Worked example: critiquing a short proposal

A volunteer writes a one-page proposal asking a local business to sponsor a school event. They paste it with the prompt: reader is a busy shop owner who has not met them, goal is a yes or a meeting. The critique says the main point appears in paragraph three, the benefits to the business are vague, and there is no clear next step. It quotes the sentences that cause each problem and ranks them.

The volunteer moves the request to the opening, replaces "great exposure" with specific details of how the sponsor would be recognized, and ends with an offer to visit the shop. Notice that the AI never wrote the proposal. It acted like a reader who could say where they got lost, and the volunteer made the changes with their own knowledge of the event.

## Getting feedback you can trust more

Ask for evidence every time: "quote the exact sentence" prevents vague comments. Request a confidence level when the advice depends on facts, such as "this statistic seems unsupported," and verify those points independently. Run the critique twice, in fresh chats, and keep the points that appear both times, since inconsistent comments are often noise. Finally, give the draft to a real person for the final check when the stakes are high, such as an application, a thesis chapter or a public statement.

## Common mistakes

- **Not naming the reader.** Feedback becomes generic.
- **Allowing rewrites too early.** You lose your voice and the learning.
- **Accepting all suggestions.** Some will conflict with your purpose.
- **Asking for praise.** "Is this good?" invites flattery.
- **Skipping the rubric.** Missing requirements go unnoticed.
- **Treating one critique as final.** Seek human feedback for important work.

## Next steps

Pair this method with the editing prompts in the [writing collection](/prompts/category/writing), draft your own critique template in the [prompt builder](/prompt-builder), and check job documents with the [ATS resume checker](/ats-resume-checker).

title: Reusable Prompt Templates: How to Use Variables and Slots
excerpt: Turn one-off prompts into reusable templates with variables, defaults and fixed rules, so you get consistent AI results on repeat tasks in seconds.
seo_title: Reusable Prompt Templates With Variables and Slots
seo_description: Learn to build reusable prompt templates with variables, defaults and fixed rules. Includes patterns for emails, summaries and study tasks you can copy today.

faq.q: What is a prompt template?
faq.a: A prompt template is a prompt with fixed instructions and marked slots for the parts that change, such as topic, audience or length. You fill the slots each time, so quality stays consistent and you save time.

faq.q: How many variables should a template have?
faq.a: Usually three to six. Too few and the template is not flexible; too many and filling it in takes longer than writing a fresh prompt. Keep variables for details that truly change between uses.

faq.q: How do I name variables clearly?
faq.a: Use descriptive capital words in brackets, such as [AUDIENCE] or [WORD LIMIT], and keep them identical across your templates. Add a short hint inside the brackets when the expected format is not obvious.

faq.q: Can I use templates in any AI tool?
faq.a: Yes. Templates are just text. You can store them in a notes app or document and paste them into any chat tool. Some tools also offer saved instructions or custom assistants for reuse.

content:
A reusable prompt template is a prompt where the instructions stay fixed and the details that change are replaced by labeled slots. Fill the slots, paste, and you get a consistent result without rewriting the prompt each time.

Templates are what turn a lucky prompt into a dependable tool. Here is how to design them well.

## Fixed parts and variable parts

Every good template separates two things.

- **Fixed parts:** the rules that make the output good every time, such as format, tone guidelines, "use only the text provided," and what to do when information is missing.
- **Variable parts:** details that change per task, such as the topic, audience, length, input text and deadline.

Locking the fixed parts means you never forget the rule that prevents a common failure. Exposing only the variables keeps filling the template quick.

## Slot naming conventions

Pick a convention and keep it everywhere.

- Capital letters in square brackets: [TOPIC], [AUDIENCE], [WORD LIMIT].
- A short hint after a colon when needed: [TONE: friendly / formal / neutral].
- A default in the hint: [LENGTH: 150 words].
- A separate label for pasted material: [PASTE TEXT HERE].

When you see [AUDIENCE] in any template, you know what belongs there.

## A basic template, step by step

Start with a prompt that worked well.

Original:

```
Write an email to my professor asking for an extension on my essay because I was ill.
Make it polite and short.
```

Step one: find the parts that change: recipient, reason, assignment, new date, tone, length.
Step two: replace them with slots.
Step three: add fixed rules that prevent problems.

```
Write an email.
Recipient: [WHO, e.g. professor / manager]
Purpose: [REQUEST, e.g. ask for a deadline extension]
Reason (keep it brief and truthful): [REASON]
Details to include: [ASSIGNMENT / DATE / PROPOSED NEW DATE]
Tone: [TONE: polite and professional]
Length: [LENGTH: under 120 words]

Rules:
- Put the request in the first two sentences.
- Do not invent facts or excuses beyond what I provided.
- End with a clear next step.
- Give me a subject line.
```

The "do not invent facts" rule is fixed because you always want it.

## Template patterns worth keeping

### The summarizer

```
Summarize the text for [AUDIENCE] in [FORMAT, e.g. 5 bullets].
Prioritize: [WHAT MUST BE KEPT].
Use only the text. Mark unclear points "unclear in source."
Text: [PASTE TEXT HERE]
```

### The explainer

```
Explain [CONCEPT] to [LEVEL, e.g. a 12-year-old / a college beginner].
Use one everyday analogy and one worked example.
Then give me 3 questions to test my understanding, with answers.
```

### The critic

```
Review the [DOCUMENT TYPE] below for [READER].
Rank the 3 biggest problems with quotes. Do not rewrite.
Draft: [PASTE TEXT HERE]
```

### The planner

```
Create a [TIME FRAME] plan to achieve [GOAL].
Available time: [HOURS PER DAY/WEEK]. Constraints: [CONSTRAINTS].
Output a table: Day/Week | Task | Time | Check that it is done.
```

For a study version of the planner, the [study planner](/study-planner) builds schedules directly.

## Add optional blocks

Some details only matter sometimes. Mark them as optional.

```
[OPTIONAL: Use this style sample to match my voice: ...]
[OPTIONAL: Avoid these words: ...]
```

When you do not need an optional block, delete the whole line before pasting. Leftover empty brackets can confuse the model, so scan the final prompt before sending.

## Include an example slot

Examples are powerful, and a template can reserve space for one.

```
Example of the style I want (match the style, do not copy the content):
[PASTE EXAMPLE OR DELETE THIS LINE]
```

This stays flexible: with an example the output follows it, without one the model uses the instructions alone.

## Test the template

A template is only useful if it works across inputs.

1. Fill it with three different realistic cases.
2. Read each output and score it on what you care about.
3. Where one fails, find the missing rule or the unclear slot.
4. Fix and retest on all three.

If the template only works for the example you built it from, it is not yet a template; it is a single prompt with blanks.

## Keep templates short and readable

Long templates with dozens of rules become hard to maintain, and models can lose track of details. Aim for a template you can read in half a minute. If you need many rules, consider splitting the task into steps, as in our guide to [multi-step prompt workflows](/blog).

## Document each template

Beside every saved template, add:

- when to use it,
- what each slot expects,
- what to check in the output,
- a version note.

This is the difference between a pile of prompts and a working [prompt library](/blog).

## Using built-in tools

Some AI tools let you save custom instructions or create reusable assistants, and names and limits vary by product. Check the tool's official help to see what is available. The [prompt builder](/prompt-builder) on this site can also help you structure the slots.

## Avoid sensitive data in templates

Keep real names, client details and private information out of the saved template. Use placeholders and fill in only what is needed, as covered in our [privacy-safe prompting guide](/blog).

## Worked example: a weekly update template

Suppose you send a weekly progress update to a supervisor. Instead of writing a new prompt each Friday, you save this: "Write a weekly update for [RECIPIENT] in [TONE]. Include three sections: Done this week: [LIST]. Blocked or at risk: [LIST]. Plan for next week: [LIST]. Keep it under [LENGTH]. Use only the items I listed. Do not add achievements or dates. Start with a one-sentence summary."

On Friday you paste your bullet points into the slots and the output matches the format your supervisor expects, every week, in under a minute. The fixed rule "use only the items I listed" protects you from the model embellishing your work, which would be both inaccurate and embarrassing.

## Versioning slots over time

As you use a template, you will notice slots you always fill the same way and details you keep forgetting to supply. Convert the constant ones into fixed text and promote the forgotten ones into slots. Occasionally add a "notes" slot labeled [ANYTHING ELSE THE MODEL SHOULD KNOW] for unusual cases, so you do not need to edit the template body. After a month of use, a good template feels almost invisible: you know exactly what to put in, and the result comes out right.

## Common mistakes

- **Too many slots.** Filling them takes longer than writing a new prompt.
- **Unclear slot names.** [INFO] could mean anything.
- **Leaving brackets in the final prompt.** Stray placeholders can derail the output.
- **Testing on one input.** The template may break on others.
- **No fixed safety rules.** Always keep "do not invent" and "use only provided text" where facts matter.
- **Never updating.** Review and improve templates as you learn what fails.

## Next steps

Create your first template in the [prompt builder](/prompt-builder), browse proven structures in the [prompt library](/prompts), and adapt writing formats from the [writing prompts](/prompts/category/writing).

title: Turn Messy Notes Into a Study Guide With AI Prompts
excerpt: Convert scattered lecture notes into a clean study guide with AI. Prompts for organizing, flagging gaps, making flashcards and practice questions to verify.
seo_title: Turn Messy Notes Into a Study Guide With AI Prompts
seo_description: Turn messy lecture notes into an organized study guide with AI: prompts to structure notes, flag gaps, build flashcards and practice questions, and verify it.

faq.q: Can AI turn my class notes into a study guide?
faq.a: Yes. Paste your notes and ask it to organize them into headings, key terms and questions using only your content. Then check the result against your textbook or lecture materials, since AI may smooth over errors.

faq.q: How do I stop AI adding information that was not in my notes?
faq.a: Tell it to use only your notes and mark gaps instead of filling them. Add a rule like 'if something is unclear, write [unclear]'. Then fill gaps yourself from reliable course materials.

faq.q: Are AI-made flashcards good for studying?
faq.a: They can be, if the facts are correct and each card tests one idea. Review every card before use, and make some yourself, since creating questions is itself a strong way to learn.

faq.q: Is using AI to make a study guide cheating?
faq.a: Organizing your own notes for personal study is generally acceptable, but rules differ by course. Do not submit AI-generated material as your own graded work, and check your instructor's policy on AI use.

content:
To turn messy notes into a study guide, paste them into an AI tool and ask it to organize them using only your content, flag anything unclear, and then generate key terms and practice questions. Verify the result against your course materials before you rely on it.

This works well because notes are often fragmented: half sentences, missing links between ideas, topics out of order. AI is good at imposing structure. It is not good at knowing what your instructor emphasized, so you stay in charge of the content.

## Step 1: Prepare your raw notes

Before prompting:

- Gather notes from one topic or lecture at a time.
- Remove personal data and anything unrelated.
- Mark things you already know are uncertain with a "?".
- Add the course name, level and exam format so the model can aim the guide correctly.

Smaller chunks produce more accurate guides than a whole semester pasted at once.

## Step 2: Organize without adding

```
Below are my raw lecture notes for [COURSE, LEVEL].
Reorganize them into a clear study guide with headings and bullet points.

Rules:
- Use ONLY information in my notes. Do not add new facts.
- Keep my terminology.
- If a point is incomplete or unclear, keep it and mark it [unclear].
- If two parts seem to contradict each other, list them under "Possible conflicts."
- Keep the original order unless a different order is clearly more logical; if you change it, tell me.

Notes:
[PASTE]
```

The "Possible conflicts" instruction is useful. Your notes may contain errors from rushed handwriting, and surfacing contradictions gives you a place to start checking.

## Step 3: Fill the gaps yourself

Review everything marked [unclear] and every conflict. Look up answers in your textbook, slides or class resources. If you want AI help, supply the reliable text:

```
Here is the relevant textbook passage. Use it to clarify the [unclear] items in my
study guide. Show which sentence of the passage supports each clarification.
```

Avoid asking the AI to fill gaps from its own memory, since it may produce plausible but wrong details that match no part of your course.

## Step 4: Extract key terms

```
From the study guide, list all key terms with a one-sentence definition each,
using only the guide. Group them by topic. Flag any term whose definition is weak.
```

Compare the definitions with your course glossary. Precise wording matters in many exams.

## Step 5: Build a concept map in text

Understanding how ideas connect is more valuable than memorizing isolated facts.

```
Describe how the main concepts in the guide relate. Use a simple outline showing:
cause -> effect, part -> whole, and compare/contrast pairs.
Then list the three ideas an exam would most likely test, based only on emphasis in my notes.
```

The last line is a guess based on your notes, not on your actual exam. Compare it with your instructor's hints.

## Step 6: Generate practice questions

Active recall beats rereading.

```
Write 12 practice questions from the study guide:
- 5 recall, 4 application, 3 "explain why".
Do not show answers yet. After I answer, I will ask you to mark them.
```

Answer from memory first. Then request the key.

```
Here are my answers. Mark each as correct, partly correct or incorrect,
using only the study guide as the standard, and say what I missed.
```

If the guide is wrong, the marking will be wrong too, so any disagreement should send you back to the course materials.

## Step 7: Flashcards that work

Good flashcards test one idea each. Ask for a table:

```
Create 20 flashcards from the guide as a table: Front (question) | Back (short answer).
One idea per card. No yes/no questions. Include a mix of definitions and "why" questions.
```

Delete weak cards, rewrite unclear ones and add your own. Writing a few yourself reinforces the memory.

## Step 8: Schedule the revision

A guide is only useful if you review it on a plan. Spread sessions over several days and revisit difficult topics. The [study planner](/study-planner) helps you build a schedule around your exam date, or you can ask the AI to draft one from your available hours and then adjust.

## Check before trusting

- Compare key facts, formulas and definitions with your textbook.
- Look for oversimplified explanations that leave out conditions.
- Make sure the guide matches what your instructor emphasized.
- Ask a classmate or teacher about anything still unclear.

## Study ethics

Using AI to organize your own notes for your own revision is a different thing from having it produce graded work. Follow your course and school policies, do not share paid course materials in ways that break their terms, and avoid pasting classmates' private notes without permission.

## Worked example: a biology lecture

A student pastes notes on cell respiration that read: "glycolysis cytoplasm 2 ATP net?? krebs in matrix, NADH carries e-, ETC makes most ATP, needs O2 - why?" The organizing prompt returns headings for each stage, with location, inputs and outputs listed where the notes support them. It marks "2 ATP net" as [unclear] because of the question marks, and "why needs O2" as an open question.

The student then checks the textbook, confirms the figure, and answers the open question using the book's explanation about oxygen as the final electron acceptor. The final guide contains information the student verified, laid out clearly. The AI saved formatting time, and the student did the learning where it counts: resolving the unclear points.

## Using the guide for active recall

Reading a neat guide feels productive but teaches less than testing yourself. Cover the answers and quiz yourself from the flashcards. Explain a section aloud as if teaching a friend. Rewrite a topic from memory, then compare it with the guide and mark the gaps. Ask the AI to produce "tricky variations" on a question type once you can answer the basic ones. Space your sessions over several days, and shift the time you spend toward items you got wrong. Over a week this beats a single long reading session.

## A quick study guide checklist

When the guide is ready, confirm that every key term has a definition you verified, that each topic has at least one practice question, that the unclear items are resolved, and that you have a revision date set for each section. If you cannot explain a section without looking at it, it is not yet learned, and that is the section to revisit first.

## Common mistakes

- **Letting AI fill gaps from memory.** Errors enter your study material.
- **Pasting everything at once.** Quality drops with huge inputs.
- **Reading the guide passively.** Test yourself with questions.
- **Not verifying.** A neat guide can still be wrong.
- **Skipping your own effort.** Making summaries and questions yourself builds understanding.
- **Ignoring policy.** Course rules about AI vary.

## Next steps

Browse more revision templates in the [student prompts](/prompts/category/students), plan your sessions with the [study planner](/study-planner), and build a tailored request with the [prompt builder](/prompt-builder).

title: Compare Options With AI: Decision Table Prompts That Work
excerpt: Use AI to structure tough choices. Learn prompts that build criteria, weighted comparison tables and devil's-advocate checks, while you keep the final decision.
seo_title: Compare Options With AI: Decision Table Prompts
seo_description: Use AI to compare options clearly: define criteria, build weighted decision tables, test assumptions and argue against your top pick. Prompt templates included.

faq.q: Can AI make decisions for me?
faq.a: It can organize information and test your reasoning, but it does not know your full situation or values and can be wrong. Use it to structure the choice, then decide yourself, and consult a professional for legal, medical or financial decisions.

faq.q: What is a weighted decision table?
faq.a: It is a table that lists options as rows and criteria as columns, with each criterion given a weight for importance. You score each option, multiply by the weights and compare totals, which makes trade-offs visible.

faq.q: How do I stop AI from being biased toward one option?
faq.a: Supply your criteria first, ask it to argue for every option fairly, and request the strongest case against your preferred choice. Check any factual claims about the options with independent sources.

faq.q: Should I trust numeric scores from AI?
faq.a: Treat them as rough opinions, not measurements. Scores depend on the information you gave and the model's judgment. Adjust them with your own knowledge and use the process to clarify priorities.

content:
To compare options with AI, first decide your criteria and their importance, then ask for a table that scores each option against them using only facts you provide. Finish by asking for the strongest argument against your top choice. The tool structures your thinking; the decision stays yours.

This works for choosing a course, comparing tools, evaluating job offers, picking a project topic or selecting a laptop. It does not work well if you outsource judgment about things only you can know, like your values and risk tolerance.

## Why a table beats a paragraph

Asked "which is better, A or B?", a model tends to produce balanced-sounding prose that hides the trade-offs. A table forces specifics: which criteria, how much each matters, what each option offers on each one. It also shows where information is missing.

## Step 1: Set your criteria first

Before showing any options, decide what matters. If you let the model choose criteria after seeing options, it may emphasize features that favor its first impression.

Ask for help, but review the list:

```
I am choosing between [OPTIONS] for [PURPOSE].
Suggest 6 to 8 criteria that matter for this decision, with a one-line explanation each.
Include criteria people commonly overlook, such as long-term costs, effort, risks and reversibility.
Do not compare the options yet.
```

Then edit: delete irrelevant criteria, add ones the model missed and rank them.

## Step 2: Assign weights

Give each criterion a weight from 1 to 5, or percentages that sum to 100. Decide yourself. The weights are where your values enter the decision. If you cannot decide, ask the model to propose weights with reasons and then change them.

## Step 3: Provide facts

For accuracy, supply the information about each option, copied from official pages, brochures or your own notes. If you rely on the model's memory, details may be outdated or wrong. If you do not have facts, ask the model to list what you should find out, rather than guess.

```
For each option, list the facts I still need to find out, and where I could find them.
Do not fill them in from memory.
```

## Step 4: Build the weighted table

```
Using ONLY the facts below, build a table.
Rows: the options. Columns: my criteria, with weights in the header.
Score each cell from 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent) and add a short reason in brackets.
If the facts do not cover a cell, write "unknown" instead of guessing.
Then calculate the weighted total for each option and show the calculation.

Criteria and weights: [LIST]
Options and facts: [PASTE]
```

Check the arithmetic in a spreadsheet, since models can slip on calculations. More important than the total is the pattern: where does each option win or lose, and are there "unknowns" that could change the result?

## Step 5: Stress-test the result

Totals can look more certain than they are. Try these checks:

- **Sensitivity:** "If I change the weight of [CRITERION] from 3 to 5, does the ranking change?" If tiny changes flip the winner, the options are close and other factors matter.
- **Missing criteria:** "What important factor have I not included?"
- **Devil's advocate:** "Make the strongest honest case against the top-scoring option."
- **Pre-mortem:** "Imagine I chose this and regret it a year later. What are the most likely reasons?"

These prompts counter the false precision of numbers.

## Step 6: Separate facts, estimates and preferences

Decisions mix three kinds of information:

1. **Facts** you can verify, such as price or duration.
2. **Estimates** about the future, such as how hard something will be.
3. **Preferences** about what you value.

Ask the model to label each cell's reason as fact, estimate or preference. Then verify facts and reconsider estimates. Preferences are yours.

## Example: choosing a study resource

Suppose you compare three courses. Your criteria might be cost, time per week, depth, practice material and recognition. You weight depth and practice highest. After scoring, you notice Course B wins narrowly, but "recognition" is unknown for two options. That tells you what to research before committing, which is more valuable than the total.

## When not to rely on AI analysis

For decisions involving health, legal rights, major finances or safety, use AI only to prepare questions and organize information. Consult a qualified professional, and do not treat a score as advice.

## Keep a record

Save the final table and your reasoning. Months later, you can see what you knew when you decided, which helps you learn from the outcome. A good template also belongs in your [prompt library](/blog).

## Worked example: comparing three laptops for study

A student has three laptops in mind and a fixed budget. They set criteria: price, battery life, weight, performance for their coursework and repair or warranty support, weighted 5, 4, 3, 4 and 2. They copy specifications from the official product pages into the prompt and ask for a table that marks unknown cells. The table shows that one model wins on battery and weight but has an unknown warranty, while another scores highest on performance but is heavier than the student wants to carry daily.

The devil's advocate prompt then points out that the top scorer's advantage depends heavily on the battery weight. The student realizes they rarely work away from a charger, lowers that weight, and the ranking shifts. The decision came from clarifying priorities, with the AI acting as a structured notepad, not as an oracle.

## Using the method for people decisions

Be careful when using this approach on decisions about people, such as ranking job candidates or students. Models can pick up and amplify bias, and such decisions often carry legal and ethical obligations. Use AI to structure your own notes against criteria set in advance, never to rank people automatically, and make sure a human reviews and owns the decision. For personal choices like picking a course or a city, the method is a good fit because the stakes and the values are yours.

## A quick decision checklist

Before you finalize, check that your criteria were set before you saw the options, that every score has a reason, and that unknown cells have a plan for being filled. Ask whether the winner still wins if the two most uncertain scores were lower. If the answer is no, gather more information before deciding. Sleep on important decisions, then reread the table with fresh eyes.

## Common mistakes

- **Choosing criteria after seeing the options.** This skews results.
- **Letting the model guess facts.** Supply sources or mark "unknown."
- **Believing precise totals.** Scores are subjective.
- **Skipping the counter-argument.** The case against your pick reveals risks.
- **Ignoring your values.** Weights should reflect you, not the model.
- **Not checking arithmetic.** Verify calculations.

## Next steps

Browse more analysis templates in the [productivity prompts](/prompts/category/productivity), set up your request in the [prompt builder](/prompt-builder), and compare tools in the [AI tools directory](/ai-tools).

title: Outline Essays and Reports With AI Without Losing Your Voice
excerpt: Use AI to plan an essay or report outline: clarify your thesis, structure arguments and spot gaps, while doing the research and writing yourself.
seo_title: Outline Essays and Reports With AI Prompts
seo_description: Use AI prompts to outline essays and reports: sharpen a thesis, organize arguments, find gaps and plan sources, while keeping the research and writing your own.

faq.q: Is using AI to make an essay outline allowed?
faq.a: It depends on your school and assignment. Many instructors allow help with planning but not with writing the submission. Read your course policy, ask if unsure, and disclose AI use when required.

faq.q: How do I get a strong thesis statement with AI?
faq.a: Give your topic, your position and the evidence you have, then ask for questions that test the thesis and a few alternative phrasings. Choose and rewrite it yourself so it reflects your own argument.

faq.q: Should I ask AI to write the whole essay from the outline?
faq.a: Not if you are being assessed on your own work. Use the outline as a plan and write the content yourself from sources you have read. Submitting generated text as your own can break academic integrity rules.

faq.q: How detailed should an outline be?
faq.a: Detailed enough that each paragraph has a clear claim, the evidence you plan to use and a link to the thesis. For a long report, add section goals and estimated word counts.

content:
Use AI to plan an essay or report, not to write it. Give it your topic, your position and the assignment requirements, ask for a structure and for weaknesses in your argument, then fill every section with your own research and writing.

A good outline saves hours because it exposes problems early: a thesis that is too broad, a section with no evidence, an argument that does not follow. AI is well suited to finding those problems.

## Check your policy first

Rules about AI in coursework vary by school, course and even assignment. Some forbid it, some allow planning help, some require a note describing how you used it. Read the instructions, ask your teacher if they are unclear and keep a brief record of what you asked. Everything below assumes you will do the thinking, reading and writing yourself.

## Step 1: Clarify the task

Paste the assignment brief and ask for an analysis, not an answer.

```
Here is my assignment brief. In your own words:
1. What exactly am I being asked to do (verbs like analyze, compare, evaluate)?
2. What are the grading criteria or hidden requirements?
3. What would a weak response look like?
Do not suggest a topic or write content.

Brief: [PASTE]
```

Misreading the question is a major cause of lost marks, and this takes two minutes.

## Step 2: Narrow your topic into a question

A topic like "social media" is not an essay. Ask for help narrowing:

```
My broad topic is [TOPIC] for a [LEVEL] [ESSAY TYPE] of [WORD COUNT] words.
Give me 8 narrower research questions of different types: descriptive, comparative,
causal and evaluative. Note which are likely too broad or too narrow for this length.
```

Pick one and adapt it. The choice should reflect your interest and the sources you can actually find.

## Step 3: Draft and stress-test a thesis

Write your own thesis first, even if rough. Then:

```
Here is my draft thesis: [THESIS]
1. Is it arguable, specific and answerable within [WORD COUNT]?
2. What are the three strongest objections a skeptical reader could raise?
3. What evidence would I need to support it?
Do not rewrite my thesis. Ask me questions if the claim is unclear.
```

Revising in response to questions keeps the argument yours.

## Step 4: Build the structure

Once you have a thesis, request a skeleton.

```
Create an outline for a [WORD COUNT] [ESSAY/REPORT] with this thesis: [THESIS].
For each section give:
- the claim it will make (one sentence),
- the kind of evidence needed (not specific facts or citations),
- how it connects to the thesis,
- a target word count.
Include where a counter-argument and response should go.
```

Asking for "kinds of evidence" rather than facts avoids invented sources. You will find real evidence yourself.

## Step 5: Map your research onto the outline

As you read real sources, add notes under each section: the source, the page, the point and a short quote or paraphrase in your words. Then ask:

```
Here is my outline and my verified notes. Which sections are well supported,
which have thin evidence, and which of my notes are not used?
Use only what I pasted.
```

You will often discover that a section needs more research or that your thesis needs to change, which is a normal and healthy part of writing.

## Step 6: Check the logic

```
Read my outline as a chain of reasoning. Identify:
- any jump where a section does not follow from the previous one,
- repeated points,
- claims that depend on an assumption I have not stated.
```

Fix these before drafting. Moving a section in an outline is far easier than rewriting a draft.

## Reports and professional documents

For reports, add practical sections: executive summary, background, method, findings, recommendations and limitations. Ask the model to adapt the structure to your audience, such as a manager who reads only the first page, and to point out where evidence or data is needed. The same discipline applies: you supply the facts.

## Writing from the outline

When you start drafting, work one section at a time in your own words. If you get stuck, ask for questions, not paragraphs: "What would a reader need to know before this point?" Then write. Afterward, use feedback prompts like those in our guide to [asking AI to critique your draft](/blog).

## Citations and references

Do not ask AI to generate references. Models can produce realistic but nonexistent sources. Find each source in a library or database, read it and cite it in your required style, using a reference manager if you have one.

## Worked example: from broad topic to outline

A student must write a 1,500-word essay on technology in education. Narrowing prompts suggest several questions, including whether classroom tablets improve reading comprehension compared with paper.
