The student picks it because they can find real studies. Their draft thesis claims tablets help. The stress-test prompt asks what a skeptic would say: that results depend on the type of task and the quality of the content, and that distraction is a factor. The student revises the thesis to a conditional claim, which is easier to defend in 1,500 words.

The outline then has four sections: context, evidence on comprehension, evidence on distraction and a conclusion with a conditional recommendation. Each section lists the kind of evidence needed. Everything else, the sources, the reading and the writing, the student does personally.

## Planning time as well as content

An outline also lets you plan the work. Assign each section a target word count and a deadline, and schedule research before writing. Allow time for revision and for checking citations, which students often leave to the last hour. Putting these tasks in the [study planner](/study-planner) turns the outline into a calendar. If a section needs more sources than you can realistically find, say so early and adjust the scope, rather than discovering the problem the night before the deadline.

## A quick outline checklist

Check that your thesis answers the exact question, that each section makes one clear claim, that you have a plan for the counter-argument, and that the word counts add up to the limit. Then confirm that you know where the evidence for each claim will come from. If any section has no source in sight, change the section or the thesis now, while it is cheap.

## Common mistakes

- **Skipping the assignment analysis.** You may answer a different question.
- **Outsourcing the thesis.** The argument should be yours.
- **Asking for specific facts and citations.** These are hallucination hotspots.
- **Over-detailed outlines that lock you in.** Allow the structure to change as you learn.
- **Writing the essay with AI and calling it planning.** That violates most integrity policies.
- **Not recording AI use.** Keep notes in case you must disclose.

## Next steps

Find planning templates in the [student prompts](/prompts/category/students), schedule your writing sessions in the [study planner](/study-planner), and shape your request with the [prompt builder](/prompt-builder).

title: How to Test and Compare Prompts: A Simple A/B Method
excerpt: Find out which prompt really works better. Use a simple A/B method with test cases, scoring criteria and notes so your prompt improvements are evidence-based.
seo_title: Test and Compare Prompts: A Simple A/B Method
seo_description: Learn a simple A/B method to test and compare prompts: build test cases, change one variable, score results with criteria and keep notes to pick a winner.

faq.q: How do I know if one prompt is better than another?
faq.a: Run both on the same set of realistic inputs, score the outputs against the same criteria, and compare patterns across all test cases. One good result proves little because AI outputs vary from run to run.

faq.q: How many test cases do I need?
faq.a: For personal use, three to five varied inputs usually reveal most problems, including at least one tricky edge case. For prompts that many people will rely on, test more and include real examples.

faq.q: Why do I get different answers from the same prompt?
faq.a: Many AI tools include randomness, so identical prompts can yield different outputs. That is why you should test several times and judge by consistency, not by a single good or bad result.

faq.q: Do I need special software to test prompts?
faq.a: No. A spreadsheet and a chat tool are enough for a basic comparison. Dedicated evaluation tools exist for large-scale testing, but the method of controlled changes and consistent scoring is the same.

content:
To tell whether one prompt is really better than another, run both on the same set of test inputs, change only one thing between them and score every output with the same criteria. Judge by patterns across several cases, not by one impressive answer.

Most people improve prompts by feel: tweak, try once, decide. That works for casual use. When a prompt will be reused or shared, a small amount of structure prevents you from keeping a version that only looked good once.

## Why single tries mislead

AI output varies. The same prompt can give a great result and a mediocre one back to back. Differences between prompts can also be small compared with that natural variation. If you compare one output from version A with one from version B, you may be comparing luck.

A fairer comparison uses several inputs and several runs.

## Step 1: Define what "better" means

Write two to five criteria before you test. Examples:

- Follows the format requested.
- Stays within the length limit.
- Factually consistent with the provided text.
- Right tone for the audience.
- Includes all required points.
- Contains no invented details.

Binary checks, pass or fail, are easiest to apply consistently. Use a 1 to 5 scale for qualities like clarity. Our guide to [evaluating answer quality](/blog) gives a ready rubric.

## Step 2: Build a small test set

Choose three to five inputs that represent real use, including difficult ones.

- A typical case.
- A short or minimal input.
- A long or messy input.
- An edge case, such as missing information or conflicting details.
- A case where the model previously failed.

Keep the inputs fixed so you can reuse them every time you modify the prompt. Remove private data before using real material.

## Step 3: Change one variable

Version B should differ from version A in one respect, so you know what caused any difference. Single changes you might test:

- adding a role or audience,
- adding an example,
- adding a length limit,
- moving rules to a numbered list,
- adding "if information is missing, say so,"
- splitting one prompt into two steps.

If you want to test five changes, run five comparisons in sequence, or accept that you will not know which one mattered.

## Step 4: Run and record

Use a simple table.

| Test case | Version | Run | Format ok | Length ok | Accurate | Tone | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Typical | A | 1 | Yes | No | Yes | 4 | Too long |
| Typical | B | 1 | Yes | Yes | Yes | 4 | |
| Edge case | A | 1 | No | No | No | 2 | Invented a date |
| Edge case | B | 1 | Yes | Yes | Yes | 3 | Said "not stated" |

Run each version at least twice per case if you can. Start a fresh chat for each run so previous messages do not influence the result.

## Step 5: Read the results for patterns

Look for questions like:

- Does B win on most cases, or only on one?
- Does a version improve one criterion but hurt another?
- Where are failures concentrated: edge cases, long inputs, a certain tone?
- Is the difference big enough to matter, or are both fine?

If results are mixed, keep the simpler prompt. Extra complexity should earn its place.

## Step 6: Check accuracy independently

Scoring "accurate" requires checking the content against the source, not trusting how it reads. A prompt that produces confident but incorrect text may score well on style and badly on truth. Verify facts in at least a sample of outputs, as described in our [fact-checking guide](/blog).

## Step 7: Decide and document

Pick the winner and save it with notes:

```
Prompt: Meeting-notes summarizer v4
Tested against: 5 transcripts (2 short, 2 long, 1 messy)
Change from v3: added "write 'not stated' for missing owners or deadlines"
Result: fewer invented owners; slightly longer outputs
Known weakness: struggles with overlapping speakers
```

Notes make your [prompt library](/blog) far more valuable, since each prompt carries its evidence and known limits.

## Using AI to generate test cases

You can ask a model to propose tricky inputs.

```
My prompt does [TASK]. Suggest 8 test inputs that could make it fail:
ambiguous wording, missing details, contradictory information, unusual formatting,
very short or very long text. For each, say what failure it targets.
```

Create the actual inputs yourself or review them for realism. Fabricated test data should not be mistaken for real-world performance.

## Comparing tools or settings

The same method applies when comparing different AI tools or modes. Keep the prompt and inputs identical, score blind if possible, and repeat across tasks. Tools and features change frequently, so avoid broad conclusions from one test, and check official documentation for current capabilities.

## Know the limits

A small test set tells you about your prompt on your type of inputs. It does not prove the prompt will always work, and it does not make output safe for high-stakes use. Keep human review where mistakes would matter.

## Worked example: testing two email prompts

You write a prompt to turn rough notes into a polite follow-up email. Version A says: "Write a polite follow-up email from these notes." Version B adds: "Under 100 words. Put the request in the first sentence. Do not add facts. If a date is missing, write [date needed]." Your test set has four note sets: a normal one, a very short one, a long messy one and one missing a date.

Version A produces warm but long emails and invents a date in the missing-date case. Version B passes the length check in all four and flags the missing date. Scoring gives a clear result, but also shows a new weakness: B's emails sound slightly curt. Your next test, version C, adds "friendly tone" and you compare again. Two rounds of small experiments gave you an evidence-backed prompt in about twenty minutes.

## Avoiding false confidence

Be honest about what a small test shows. If B beat A on four cases, you have good reason to prefer B for similar inputs, not proof that it is best or that it always works. Prompts can behave differently when the model, the tool or the settings change, so retest important prompts from time to time. If a prompt is used by others, ask them to report failures and add each one to your test set. The test set grows into a record of real cases, which is the most valuable asset in prompt work.

## Common mistakes

- **Comparing single outputs.** Variation can fool you.
- **Changing several things at once.** You cannot attribute the gain.
- **Testing only easy inputs.** Failures hide in edge cases.
- **Scoring by impression.** Use criteria written beforehand.
- **Continuing in the same chat.** Earlier messages contaminate results.
- **Not recording results.** You will repeat the same experiments.
